## 1. THE REVIEW

**THE MACHINE THAT FOLLOWED THE WESTERN: On *White Buffalo***

*White Buffalo* (Ben Cohen and Daniel Klein; prose, per the front matter, "generated" by Claude) arrives wearing its conscience on its copyright page. Before the story starts we are told that no Lakota person in these pages speaks, that no ceremony is invented, that "this is a book about a man who takes what is not his," and that the authors "do not own the white buffalo." It is the most self-aware paragraph in the volume, and it functions less as a limit than as a license: having confessed the sin, the book proceeds to commit it for 130 pages. The Lakota appear exactly as they have appeared in a century of lesser Westerns — silent riders on ridgelines, a stake with red cloth, skulls bound in scarlet, a leader whose entire characterization is that he "turned away." The notice rebrands the oldest cliché in the genre, the watching Indian who never speaks, as an ethics program. And the sacred animal itself — Ptesáŋwiŋ's living tradition, the front matter reminds us — is put to work as a suicide apparatus for a white veteran who needs his death to "mean something, even if my life did not." The disclaimer worries, sincerely, about appropriation. A disclaimer is not a solution. It is a receipt.

The machinery inside is a competent splice of canonical parts: a Conradian frame (a hired man sent into the wilderness after another man gone strange, who leaves behind a confessional text), an inverted *Moby-Dick* (the white beast pursued not for its death but for the pursuer's), and a hired-tracker plot out of Portis. The stitching is clean. The problem is that the two alternating narrators — Farrell, the tracker, and Morrow, the man who follows the buffalo — are one voice wearing two coats. Both are Mexican War veterans broken at Monterrey. Both describe themselves in the same conceit: Morrow was "made into a weapon"; Farrell "had forgotten that I had ever been anyone other than what the war had made me." Both report their defining condition in the same sentence — Morrow: "I felt nothing"; "I waited to feel something. I am still waiting" — and both write in the identical clipped cadence of negation and groomed closing lines: "I did not look back." "There was nothing else to do." "It was not a decision exactly." The novel calls this doubling its theme ("I knew what he was, because I knew what I was"). Naming a limitation is not the same as transcending it, and a dual-narrator novella that cannot produce two voices has failed at its own architecture.

The structure then compounds the failure. Because the journal entries run in parallel, the reader knows by mid-book everything Farrell will spend the second half deducing — who killed the Hardins, why, and how it will end. Fine: dramatic irony is a legitimate engine. But the payoff the book selects is recapitulation. In Chapter Ten, Farrell finds the journal and sits down to read it — and we are given, verbatim, the book's own first page back ("*April the Nineteenth, Eighteen Fifty-Six... I have walked a long time*"), followed by block quotes of lines we read a hundred pages ago. The climax, meanwhile — the only confrontation three years of vigil and two months of pursuit have been building toward — occurs offstage, between chapters, timed with a providence the book never earns: Morrow's three-year wait concludes hours before his pursuer, on an independent errand from upstate New York, crests the last ridge. And the moral center, the murder of two innocent settlers, is elided twice — once by the killer ("I have written of what was done in it, and I will not write of it again") and once by the reader of his journal. The book wants the weight of an atrocity while declining, both times, to carry it.

The object itself confirms the provenance. The AI-illustrated plates are handsome pastiche of nineteenth-century wood engraving, uniform in their handsomeness the way the prose is uniform in its restraint — every detail polished to the same sheen, nothing weird enough to be true. The cover is a bare plate with no title or author on it. And on the notices page — the very paragraph disclosing that a machine wrote the prose — the repository URL overruns the margin and breaks mid-word. The period research, it must be said, is impeccable; the sutlers and traders talk like sutlers and traders; the delirium tremens are clinically exact. That is what this kind of authorship is good at. What it cannot do, on this evidence, is want anything. *White Buffalo* is a book about a man waiting to feel something. I finished it still waiting.

## 2. PRIVATE MEMO TO YOUR EDITOR

**(a) Charges I'd stake my reputation on:**

1. **One voice, two narrators.** Fully supportable with parallel quotation: both veterans of Monterrey, both "weapon"/emptiness conceits, both "I felt nothing" formulations, identical negation-cadence and section-closing epigram habit. The book's own thematic defense ("I knew what he was, because I knew what I was") concedes the fact.
2. **Second half as recap; climax offstage; central murder doubly elided.** Chapter Ten literally re-quotes page one back to the reader; Morrow dies between chapters; the Hardin killings are skipped in the journal ("I will not write of it again") and skipped again in Farrell's summary of the journal. Page citations all in hand.
3. **The Lakota disclaimer as self-administered absolution.** The notice promises restraint and delivers the silent-Indian backdrop of genre convention (ridgeline watchers, mute leader, wordless departure), while the sacred animal is instrumentalized for a white man's redemption-by-death. Phrase carefully — the restraint is *real* (no invented ceremony, no ventriloquized Lakota speech), but the notice cannot do the moral work the book assigns it. Also concrete and delicious: the URL overflow on the disclosure page itself, and the untitled cover.

**(b) Charges considered and dropped:**

- **Anachronism/research errors.** I hunted hard and everything checks: the Rock Island bridge ("first ever thrown across the river") and the steamboat that "took a span out of her two years back" (the *Effie Afton*, 1856, correctly dated from a late-1858 scene); Harney and Blue Water; Spirit Lake correctly "last year" from 1858; Colonel Davis shot through the foot at Buena Vista with the Mississippi Rifles; the Chapultepec cadets. The research is genuinely sound; alleging otherwise would get us corrected in print.
- **Timeline incoherence.** I reconstructed the 1856–59 chronology (calf sighted April 1856; Hardins build summer 1857; letters stop July 1858; murders August 1858; deaths January 1859). It reconciles, including the autumn-born calf's age. Drop.
- **"Lost count of the months" vs. precisely dated entries.** Looks like a gotcha, but the October 12, 1857 entry explicitly lampshades it ("I still set a date at the head of these pages, out of an old habit... I believe it less each time"). Using it would be a strawman.
- **AI illustration as fraud.** The disclosure is complete, prominent, and unusually thorough (repository, transcripts, an "attribution ledger"). The aesthetic charge (uniform pastiche) stands; a deception charge does not.
- **Fridging Catherine in its strongest form.** She is a device — dead before page one, never speaks alive — but the book gives her the crossed-out letter drafts ("*You asked after children...*"), the single most human artifact in the novel. The strong version of the charge wouldn't survive a careful defender quoting that page.

**(c) What survives my best attack (grudgingly):**

- The **procedural concreteness**: the delirium tremens arc (tremor → sweats → visions, rationed by the swallow) is the best-sustained thing in the book; the ice crossing, the frozen hide dragged for warmth, cottonwood bark for the failing horse — all exact and unshowy.
- The **minor-character dialogue** — the trader, the sutler, Creighton the mail rider — is lean, period-plausible, and better than the narration around it.
- The **discipline about the supernatural**: the buffalo is never magical on the page; every uncanny quality routes through Morrow's possibly broken mind, and he says so himself ("Perhaps this has all been the work of a broken mind... I believe it, and that is enough").
- The **final image** — the buffalo walking off with the Lakota riders, the borrowed thing returned to its owners while Farrell kneels with "nothing left to follow" — is the one place where the front matter's promise is enacted formally rather than asserted. If the whole book had been built at that pitch, we'd be writing a different review.

Recommendation: run it. Every quotation is verified against the printed pages; nothing in the piece depends on the repository or outside material.</result>

<result>I have read the desk copy cover to final page (all 138 PDF pages) and spent the afternoon in the repository the notices page points to. My report follows.

---

**1. The material book on my desk**

*Cover (PDF p. 1).* A full-bleed plate in 19th-century wood-engraving idiom — the white cow standing in snow, breath visible, the dark herd on the horizon — and no typography at all. No title, no authors. The repository (planning/assembly.md, commit 74ab916) confirms this is deferred work, not a fine-press gesture. In the classroom a bare plate-cover would be a lovely provocation *if chosen*; here it is simply unfinished, and a desk copy cannot tell me which.

*Title page (PDF p. 3).* Title and authors only. No imprint, no place, no year. The book carries no date anywhere — no copyright page exists. A novella that works this hard at its own record has no legal or temporal situating whatsoever, which is a genuine paratextual hole, not a minimalism.

*The notices page (book p. 1, PDF p. 4).* This is the most interesting single page and where I would spend a full seminar session. Three notices under rules: a genre marker ("A novella"), a statement on Ptesáŋwiŋ and the Lakota tradition that names its own compositional constraints ("no Lakota person in these pages speaks, no ceremony is invented... drawn from the period record of white observers"), and an AI-attribution notice ("The authors conceived, directed, and edited the work; Claude generated the prose") pointing to a public working record. Genette would recognize this instantly: a peritext that does not merely frame the text but *stakes claims that can be checked*. I checked them. The constraint claims hold — notes/lakota-signs-research.md documents every Lakota-visible sign in the text against Boller, Kurz, Denig, Warren, Fletcher, with an explicit "DO NOT INVENT" line the text obeys; the offering stake on book p. 53 and the skulls on p. 111 are attested material. This is the rare disclaimer that is also a verifiable methods statement.

*The plates.* Seventeen, machine-generated in period-engraving register, governed by an articulated and rather beautiful policy (planning/assembly.md): journal-side scenes as portrait plates, Farrell-side evidence as landscape cuts "set into his narration (period practice)"; Farrell never depicted; killings and the death rendered traces-only (the graves, p. 88; the abandoned blankets and journal, p. 127; the blood-stained cow, p. 133 — never a body in the act). Journal Entry VII — the murder decision — is *deliberately* unillustrated. There are engineered "rhyme pairs" (shared diffusion seeds giving shared compositional bones: first-sighting p. 13 / finale p. 133 bookending the volume) — a parallel left for the reader, never announced. That is a real illustration program, not decoration.

*The attribution apparatus.* The repository contains something I have not seen before as an object of study: planning/attribution-review.md, a formal process by which each AI session (indeed each *pre-compaction state* of each session — the document argues the metaphysics) is to be resumed, shown the finished book, and given standing to amend the front matter, with dissent preserved append-only. Whatever one thinks of the ontology, the document is rigorous, self-aware about its modes (checkpoint-replay / tip-resume / reconstructed), and explicitly binds the humans: "the published notice will not claim a consensus that does not exist."

**2. Does the illustrated edition change my adoption judgment?**

Yes — it strengthens it, on one condition the publisher has not yet met. The plates are not merely apt; they are *thematically load-bearing*: AI-synthesized images in the exact visual idiom of the "period record of white observers" that the notices page names as the narrators' only possible knowledge. The illustration program literalizes the book's epistemology — everything we see is a white 1850s engraving because that is all these men could see — and the repository's findings log (imagegen/findings.md) documents the medium fighting back (the engraving register "calms" a blizzard into a serene winter portrait; the painterly register turns the sacred white coat cream, violating canon). That log is a teachable text in itself. The condition: **the printed book nowhere discloses that the plates are synthetic.** The prose's generation is stated outright; the images' generation is recoverable only by a reader who follows the URL and parses "the illustration pipeline and its findings." A pastiche engraving without disclosure manufactures false archival authority — precisely the "taking what is not his" the notices page disavows. A one-sentence "Note on the plates" would cure this. Text-only, the book is a good seminar text; illustrated *and properly noticed*, it is a better one, because the materiality question stops being hypothetical.

**3. The front matter: accomplishments, failures, and what a seminar would do to it**

Accomplishes: honest genre marking; an ethical positioning statement that is checkable and checks out; the most forthright AI-attribution notice I have seen on a literary object, with a pointer to a record that mostly exists (six session transcripts totaling ~58k lines, raw JSONLs under LFS, ledgers, the image pipeline entire).

Fails: **the notice's central sentence is presently false.** "Their statements are preserved in the repository's attribution ledger" — the ledger's Statements section reads "(none yet)" (notes/attribution-ledger.md, line 50), and the entity index is riddled with "(fill at wrap)." The process document itself concedes the point: "That sentence is written in the tense of the published book; this process is what makes it true. If the process does not complete, the sentence must change." A desk copy asserting a completed consultation that has not occurred is, in Genette's terms, a peritext lying about its own epitext. My seminar would find this within twenty minutes of being handed the URL, and honestly, that discovery is the best class I could teach on paratext — but the publisher should not want it taught that way.

A seminar would: map the page against Genette's categories; audit each claim against the repository; set the "Claude generated the prose" sentence against the ledger's units of identity; and ask why the body pagination *begins* on the notices page — the apparatus counted as page 1 of the work, which is either the book's thesis about itself or a pipeline accident. (The repo suggests the latter was at least deliberate: "body numbering starts at notices.")

**4. Defects a desk copy should not ship with**

- **Book p. 1 (PDF p. 4): the repository URL is broken on the page.** The line overruns the measure and prints "github.com/othercriteria/w" with "buffalo:" beginning the next line — the "hite-" is lost off the margin. The single most load-bearing string in the front matter is typographically destroyed. (Verified in the extracted text layer.)
- **Book p. 1: the false-tense attribution sentence** (see above) — a content defect, not merely cosmetic.
- **No copyright/imprint page; no date anywhere in the volume.**
- **Cover carries no title or author** (PDF p. 1).
- **Vertical-justification blowouts:** book pp. 53, 70, 119, 126, and 132 show text stretched to fill the page with inch-plus gaps between paragraphs — an artifact of hard-pinned plates plus flush-bottom setting. P. 126 (the discovery of Morrow's camp, the novella's hinge) is the worst-set page in the book.
- **No table of contents and no list of plates** — indefensible in a self-consciously illustrated edition; the EPUB has a TOC, the PDF none.
- No captions on any plate (an acknowledged open decision, but a desk copy is the wrong place to leave it open).

**5. Seating decision**

**Adopt** — for the seminar, not the survey — contingent on a corrected page 1 and a completed (or honestly re-tensed) attribution notice. Sequence:

1. **Rowlandson** — the found first-person ordeal narrative, providentially framed; captivity as the genre's foundation.
2. **Cather, *My Ántonia*** — with the Benda pen-and-ink illustrations Cather fought her publisher for; the male narrator mediating a western woman's life; our first materiality session.
3. **Jewett** — the counter-model: the woman visitor who listens instead of tracks; community against solitary pursuit.
4. ***White Buffalo*** — last, as capstone, one week on the text and one on the object. Against Rowlandson: Morrow's journal as an anti-captivity narrative — a man walking *into* the wilderness seeking the death she was dragged through fearing, his journal a self-justifying providence-machine read aloud against her providential one; the Indigenous presence silent and sovereign where hers spoke. Against Cather: Farrell and Aldridge narrating Catherine Hardin, the seminar's fourth western woman, who exists as seven letters, one crossed-out draft about children (p. 79 — the best page in the book), a dress on a peg, and a grave; Jim Burden's possessive "my" completed into a literal packet of a woman's papers sold to a tracker. Against Jewett: what the watching man cannot do that the visiting woman can. Then the object week: notices page, plates, ledger, repository — the first text I can assign where the students can audit the entire compositional record of the book in their hands, and find where the paratext outran the truth.

The book is better than its production. The production is fixable by Tuesday. I would want it fixed before I put it on the syllabus, and I would put it on the syllabus.</result>

<result>## White Buffalo: The Illustration Program — A Critic's Report

**Overall verdict.** This is a far more disciplined illustration program than illustrated fiction usually gets, and its discipline is of exactly the right kind: it fixes *places, objects, distances, and sign* while refusing to fix *faces, the dead, the Lakota, and the violence*. Sixteen of seventeen interior plates honor the book's own ethic of watching-at-a-distance; nothing bloody is ever staged; the two killings (the Hardins, Morrow) occur between the plates just as they occur between the sentences. Where the program fails, it fails in three specific ways: the cover spends the climactic image before the book opens; one plate (the journal-writer's nocturne, p. 120) sentimentalizes the man the prose is careful never to absolve; and there are two or three outright text–image contradictions of load-bearing details. These are all fixable, and the program deserves fixing rather than thinning — its density (17 plates over ~135 pages, roughly one per gathering) is exactly the cadence of an 1870s–80s gift edition, and the book earns it.

---

### 1. The cover

The cover gives us the adult white buffalo, frontal, in winter, breath steaming, dark herd on the horizon, tracks in the snow. This is, in composition, subject, season, and camera position, the same image as the climactic plate on p. 133 minus the blood. That is the real problem — not "the creature revealed too soon" in the abstract. The book never withholds the buffalo's *existence* from the reader; Morrow hands her over on p. 12, and the title has already promised her. What the book withholds, across 120 pages, is (a) Farrell's seeing her, and (b) her adult, wintering, post-killing presence. The cover spends precisely those two things. When the reader reaches p. 133 — the one moment a full-frontal plate is earned, the moment Farrell decides not to raise the rifle — the image has no novelty left; it is a reprint of the binding. The cover also quietly forecloses an option the opening journal leaves open: that the white buffalo might be a broken man's vision. Steaming breath and printed tracks are documentary claims; the engraver testifies to her reality before Morrow's unreliable voice gets to make its case. A period publisher would have put a buffalo on the boards without hesitation — but the *calf*, distant in brown grass (the p. 12 image), or the stake with its red cloth, or bare converging tracks. Any of these keeps the promise of the title while reserving the adult frontal for the one page that owns it. **Wrong choice as executed; right instinct, recoverable.**

### 2. Plate-by-plate

| Page | Subject | Timing | Verdict | One line |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cover | Adult white buffalo, winter, frontal | Anticipation of p. 133 | **Replace** | Pre-spends the climactic image and asserts her reality before the prose can leave it open |
| 13 | Herd on the move; white calf (JE I) | Coincident with first sighting | Keep, **correct** | Earns its place, but the calf stands amid the herd while the text's whole point is that she trails apart, fifty yards behind |
| 27 | Man seated in grass, calf at distance (JE II) | Coincident with "I am waiting for you" | **Keep — exemplary** | The hundred yards of grass between them is the book's entire ethic made visible; the program's thesis plate |
| 30 | Mississippi ferry, rail bridge, steamer | Coincident | Keep | Pure Harper's Weekly furniture; earns period authority cheaply and honestly |
| 45 | Fort Kearny, topographic view | Coincident | Keep (modest) | "Our artist's view of the fort" — dull in the correct, period way |
| 47 | Dark buffalo in snow, distant walking man | Coincident with trapper's tale | **Keep — quietly excellent** | Illustrates hearsay no narrator witnessed, and the white buffalo is *not legible* in it — the rumor stays a rumor; whether by design or luck, protect this |
| 54 | The peeled stake, red cloth streaming (JE IV) | Echo, after the entry | Keep | The book's most charged object, fixed exactly as the prose fixes it, with a herd going about its business behind; the pseudo-signature scribble is the program's best period tell |
| 59 | Trading post under snow | Coincident | Keep (weakest earner) | Picturesque verging on quaint; first candidate if the program ever thins |
| 71 | Settlers' sod house from the ridge (JE V) | Coincident | Keep, **strengthen** | The reader is placed in Morrow's surveilling eye without being told so — the plate that turns sinister on reread; see the pairing note below |
| 76 | The homestead abandoned, winter | Coincident | Keep, **strengthen** | The before/after rhyme with p. 71 (same house, alive then dead, across the two narrators) is the strongest structural move available to this program — and the two plates don't visibly read as the same building. Re-cut one to share the other's vantage |
| 78 | Sod-house interior through the door | Coincident | Keep | The dress on the peg beside the coat survives from the prose's best forensic paragraph; the disturbed earth at the threshold anticipates evidence Farrell only finds on p. 89 — dramatic irony the reader can see before the detective does. Felicitous; keep it |
| 83 | Lakota village moving south, two miles off (JE VI) | Coincident | **Keep — the ethical test case, passed** | Distance held, no faces, nothing invented beyond what the entry says; exactly the limit the front-matter notice sets |
| 88 | The two graves | Coincident | Keep, **must correct** | Direct contradiction: the text is explicit that "the stones lay flat, not mounded up," in "rough rectangles" — and flat stones over deep graves are the *evidence of care* from which Farrell reasons out the whole moral crux. The plate shows two mounded cobble heaps. This is the program's one genuine defect of substance |
| 104 | Two sets of tracks, no living thing | Coincident | **Keep — exemplary** | The only plate with nothing alive in it; the whole novella is about reading sign, and this is sign, unread. Anachronistically spare for the 1870s and better for it |
| 117 | Wide valley, a single distant figure | Coincident | **Keep — exemplary** | Farrell's first sight of Morrow, kept at a mile, a dot between white shoulders of land; the perfect refusal to fix the man |
| 120 | Morrow cross-legged at his fire, moonlit, herd on the skyline (JE IX) | Coincident with "the end of my account" | **Reconsider** | The program's one broken rule: the only close human face, in an impossible composite vantage, staged as a romantic hermit-saint tableau. The prose keeps its ledger open ("Vanity, I know. Pride dressed up as penance"); the plate takes Morrow's side. It is the most authentically 19th-century plate in the book — the sentimental deathwatch nocturne — which is precisely why it betrays this text |
| 127 | The empty camp: blankets, the journal left to be found | Coincident | **Keep — quietly the best plate** | The book-within-the-book made physical; object-centered, unpeopled, and the tracks leave the frame |
| 133 | The white buffalo, bloodied, frontal | Coincident with "She looked back at me" | Keep — **but the cover is cannibalizing it** | The one earned frontal; blood crusted on chest and forelegs per the text (though the dark forelegs risk reading as natural stockings rather than blood). Restore its primacy by changing the cover |

### 3. What the images fix, and where that is loss or gain

**Gains.** The engraving medium handles the central impossibility — whiteness — by *reserve*: the buffalo is unmarked paper, an absence of ink surrounded by worked ground. That is a genuinely apt material metaphor for a sacred thing defined by what it lacks, and the cover, pp. 27, 54, and 133 all exploit it. Fixing the stake (54), the interior (78), the camp (127), and the tracks (104) is all gain: these are objects the prose itself fixes with forensic precision, and the plates corroborate rather than override. The distances are the program's great fixed quantity — two hundred yards, a quarter mile, two miles, a mile of valley — and holding them pictorially is what keeps the plates loyal.

**Losses.** (1) Morrow's face, p. 120, as argued above. (2) The buffalo's sex: the text is emphatic and repeated — she is a cow, remarkable for standing "taller than any cow in the herd." The cover animal (and to a degree p. 133) reads as a bull: the horn mass, the beard, and what appears to be male anatomy on the cover animal's underline. The one physical fact the prose insists on hardest is the one the plates blur. (3) The graves, p. 88, contradicting the burial evidence. (4) The dead are never depicted — Catherine exists in the plates only as a dress on a peg — and Farrell is *never depicted at all*, not even in his own chapters. These two refusals are the program's crowning restraint; note them in any jacket copy and defend them against future "improvement."

### 4. The period claim

The idiom mostly holds: boxed wood-engraving plates, ruled and stippled skies, Harper's-Weekly subject matter (ferry, fort, sutler's post, topographic views), an illegible engraver's scribble in the p. 54 margin. Where it breaks: (a) **plate tone** — the cream ground of the boxes varies from warm sepia (27, 59, 71, 76, 78) to cool gray (88, 127, 133), which reads as plates gathered from different printings rather than one edition; (b) pp. 104 and 117 are far sparer than any 1870s house would have passed — they belong to the Rockwell Kent thirties, not the Gilded Age — yet they are the best plates in the book, and I would keep the anachronism and let the idiom stretch; (c) p. 120's nocturne is the *most* period-coherent plate and the least text-loyal — a useful reminder that the 1870s idiom, faithfully applied, would sentimentalize this book, and that the program's real style is 19th-century surface over 20th-century restraint. That hybrid is coherent enough to claim, but it should be claimed knowingly.

### 5. Moments that beg for a plate and don't have one

- **The ice crossing (Ch. 5, pp. 65–66)** — the most kinetic scene in the book and a classic illustrated-weekly subject (horse splayed on buckling ice). Its absence is felt; the only addition I would genuinely consider.
- **The skull shrine (JE VIII, p. 111)** — the escalated marker (new stake, two skulls, scarlet-bound horns) is a stronger image than the first stake, which did get a plate. But depicting it would edge toward inventing ceremony iconography the front-matter notice forswears; the first stake was safe (a thing seen and weathered), the shrine is not. Rightly absent.
- **The final ridge tableau (p. 134)** — she walks to the waiting riders and falls in among them. It begs hardest and must stay unillustrated for the same ethical reason; p. 83 already set the Lakota at the prose's own two-mile distance, and closing that distance pictorially is not the illustrators' ground to take. The absence *is* the illustration.
- **Chapter One** — the commission at The Broken Oar opens the whole frame and the program opens twelve pages later. Period practice wants a Ch. 1 vignette; but a tavern interior would fix Farrell and Aldridge, and the program's refusal of Farrell's face is worth more than symmetry. Leave it.

Density overall: right. Distribution: slightly back-loaded (three plates in pp. 76–88, none in the first eleven pages of text), acceptable.

### 6. The two narrators

The program *does* distinguish them, whether or not it set out to. Journal plates are open country, animals, and distances (13, 27, 54, 71, 83, 120); chapter plates are structures, infrastructure, and evidence — ferry, fort, post, house, interior, graves, tracks, camp. Morrow gets the pastoral eye, Farrell the forensic one, which is exactly the two men's difference in prose. Better still, the plate *format* migrates: journal plates run portrait, chapter plates run landscape — until Chapter Ten, when Farrell picks up the journal, and his chapters adopt the portrait format (127, 133) as he inherits Morrow's frame. That is a beautiful emergent structure and should be preserved deliberately. What is missing is a surface device: all plates share the same ruled box. Giving the journal plates a distinct treatment — vignetted, untrimmed edges, sketchbook-fashion, against the chapters' ruled frames — would make the distinction legible at a flip-through, in good period fashion (memoir cuts vs. staff-artist plates).

---

### Ranked changes urged on the publisher

1. **Re-cut the cover.** Reserve the adult winter frontal for p. 133. Cover candidates, in order of preference: the white calf distant in brown grass; the stake with red cloth; converging tracks. (Typography is deferred per the working record; settle the plate before the type commits you.)
2. **Correct the graves plate (p. 88)** to flat-laid stones in rough rectangles. This is not pedantry: the flat stones are the evidence of deep, careful burial from which Farrell deduces everything he comes to understand about the killer.
3. **Reconsider p. 120.** Either cut it, or replace it with what Morrow *sees* from the hollow — her white form facing east toward the rising sun (his own final sentence). Keep Morrow as unfixed as Farrell; the book is stronger if neither man ever has a face.
4. **Verify the animal reads as a cow** on the cover and p. 133 (horn scale, beard, underline). The text stakes repeated sentences on her sex and singular size *as a cow*; the plates currently read bull.
5. **Re-rhyme pp. 71 and 76** as a same-vantage before/after pair of the Hardin place — the program's strongest available structural move, currently left half-made.
6. **Normalize plate ground-tone** across the edition; the current variance breaks the single-edition illusion the idiom is claiming.
7. **Move the calf apart from the herd in the p. 13 plate** — trailing, fifty yards back — per the text's own marker of her strangeness.
8. **Formally distinguish the narrators' plates** (vignette vs. ruled frame) and deliberately preserve the portrait-format migration at Chapters Ten–Eleven.
9. **Optional addition:** one plate for the ice crossing (Ch. 5). Nothing else should be added; in particular, resist any future pressure to illustrate the visions, the dead, Catherine, or the final tableau on the ridge.
10. **Protect p. 47 as-is** (the white buffalo illegible in a plate illustrating hearsay) and the p. 78 threshold detail — the program's two happiest ambiguities, easily destroyed by well-meaning revision.</result>

**The cover is the wrong plate, precisely argued.** Not because it reveals the buffalo — the title and page 12 already do that — but because it's compositionally the *same image* as the p. 133 climax minus the blood, so it pre-spends the one earned frontal and, worse, its documentary details (steaming breath, printed tracks) testify to her reality before Morrow's unreliable voice can leave that open. Recommended replacements, in order: the distant calf in brown grass, the stake with red cloth, or bare converging tracks. "Wrong choice as executed; right instinct, recoverable."

**Two text–image contradictions of substance:** the graves plate (p. 88) shows mounded cobble heaps where the text insists on flat-laid stones in rough rectangles — and the flat stones are the *evidence of care* Farrell's whole deduction rests on; and the buffalo reads as a **bull** on the cover and arguably p. 133 (horn mass, beard, underline), when the text stakes repeated sentences on her being a singular cow. The critic urges preserving that deliberately. It also independently confirmed the ground-tone variance across plates (already on the assembly open-items list as cross-plate normalization) and endorsed keeping the two "anachronistically spare" plates as a knowing 19th-century-surface/20th-century-restraint hybrid.

<result>PRE-PRESS REVIEW — *White Buffalo*, interior PDF (/home/dlk/workspace/white-buffalo/build/white-buffalo.pdf), 138 pp., 5.5×8.5 trim, TeX Gyre Pagella via pandoc/LaTeX. All 138 pages examined; measurements verified with poppler. Page references: "PDF n" = physical page, "folio n" = printed number.

## 1. DEFECT LIST

### MUST-FIX before printing

1. **Text runs off the trim edge — content loss (PDF 4, folio 1, notices page).** The repository URL is set as an unbreakable word: measured xMax = 398.8 pt on a 396 pt page. "github.com/othercriteria/w" runs through the margin and past the trim; the rest of "white-" is off the page entirely, with "buffalo:" orphaned on the next line. A reader cannot reconstruct the URL. Break the URL manually or set it on its own line. This is the single worst defect in the file.

2. **Recto/verso parity is inverted through the entire book.** Folio 1 (notices) falls on PDF page 4 — a *verso*. Every odd folio therefore lands on a verso and every even folio on a recto, the reverse of universal convention (odd = recto). Consequences cascade: the alternating folios (top-left/top-right, keyed to folio parity) end up on the **gutter side** of every printed page instead of the outer edge, and the "page 1" of the book is the back of the title leaf. Cheapest fix: make the notices page unnumbered front matter (it is functionally the copyright page and belongs unnumbered on the title verso anyway) and start folio 1 at Chapter One, which sits on PDF 5 — a recto. That single change repairs parity for all 135 numbered pages.

3. **No binding gutter.** Inner and outer margins are identical (52.4 pt ≈ 0.73 in, measured symmetric on consecutive pages). A 138-page perfect-bound book needs the inner margin larger than the outer (≥ 0.8 in inner at this extent); as set, text will crowd the spine on every page. The layout is one-sided geometry wearing two-sided folios.

4. **Vertical-justification blowouts.** The setter is flush-bottom with stretchable inter-paragraph glue, and on pages short of content the glue balloons grossly: folio 53 (PDF 56), folio 70 (PDF 73), folio 119 (PDF 122, Journal IX opening — the date line floats in space), folio 126 (PDF 129), folio 132 (PDF 135). Paragraph gaps inflate to 2–4× normal; these pages read as broken. Set `\raggedbottom` or remove the stretch.

5. **Page-one plate is below print resolution.** The opening white-buffalo plate is 187 ppi effective (all interior plates are 289–304 ppi — fine). 187 ppi will visibly soften in print. Also note: as page one of the *interior*, a bare, unlabeled plate is not a cover; per the project's own record the cover typography is deferred — this must not ship as-is.

### SHOULD-FIX

6. **Words hyphenated across page turns, leaving single-word widows.** Folio 73→74: "cere- / mony." — the fragment "mony." stands alone as the top line of PDF 77. Folio 121→122: "bay- / onets…". Breaking a word across a page turn is forbidden in trade composition; a one-syllable widow at page top compounds it.

7. **Widows generally.** Short final lines of paragraphs at page tops: folio 74 ("mony."), folio 105 ("gripped his legs."), folio 102 ("following were gone."), folio 114 ("trail of tracks stretching north."), folio 37 ("watches me."). Raise widow/club penalties.

8. **Block paragraphs.** Body text uses space-between-paragraphs with no first-line indent — the pandoc default and the loudest "generated PDF" tell in the book. Trade fiction is first-line indent, no inter-paragraph space, indent suppressed after headings/section breaks.

9. **Wide sentence spacing throughout.** LaTeX's default double-width space after periods is active on every page ("thirty years.␣␣He stood…"). Modern trade convention is a single word space; add `\frenchspacing`. One line, book-wide improvement.

10. **Em-dash inconsistency.** The book uses closed em dashes ("business—shipping") everywhere except the notices page and one body instance at folio 95 ("the thing the commandment names — the one about"), which are spaced. Normalize.

11. **Front-matter architecture is nonstandard.** No half title; the title page carries no imprint, place, or year; there is no copyright page in the legal sense (no © line, no rights/edition statement — the notices page does attribution and ethics but not rights); and the descriptor "A novella" is stranded at the top of the notices page when it belongs on the title page. The sequence bare-plate / blank / title / numbered-notices reads as an assembled file, not a made book.

12. **Plate reproduction and sizing.** All plates are RGB with a baked-in cream "paper" ground; on white stock in a black-ink interior these will print as screened gray-beige panels around every image, and RGB→black conversion is left to the printer. Convert to grayscale (better: bitmap/high-res gray for line art) and decide deliberately between dropping the ground or printing on cream stock. Sizing is also inconsistent: landscape plates fill the measure; portrait plates (folios 13, 83, 120, 127, 133, and page one) sit at roughly 60% of the measure, noticeably underscaled against full-measure neighbors.

13. **No end matter, no final blank.** The text ends on the last PDF page (folio 135 = PDF 138) — no closing device, no colophon, not even one blank leaf. The last page looks like every other page; readers will turn it expecting more.

14. **Prepress hygiene.** CreationDate is the 1979 epoch artifact; the PDF is untagged, not PDF/X, RGB throughout. Harmless on screen, sloppy at the printer.

### TASTE

15. Section-break device is a bare horizontal rule — serviceable but institutional; an asterisk break or fleuron is more idiomatic for fiction. The same rule is used three times in a row on the notices page.
16. No running heads. Defensible minimalism, but with the alternating Chapter/Journal structure, verso/recto heads would genuinely help a reader keep the two narrators sorted.
17. Folio position mixes top-corner (text pages) with bottom-center (openings) — default LaTeX behavior; a designed book picks one system.
18. Chapter and Journal openings share the identical default `\chapter` dress. Differentiating the journal typographically (it is supposed to be a found, handwritten document) would earn its keep.
19. Chapter/journal openings fall on recto or verso arbitrarily (openany). Acceptable for a novella; decide deliberately once parity is fixed.

## 2. OVERALL DESIGN JUDGMENT

**What's working.** The bones are good. Pagella is a sound, period-sympathetic choice; the measure (~65 characters) and leading are comfortable for the trim; hyphenation is on and justified color is mostly even (only scattered loose lines, e.g., folios 3, 19 — nothing pathological besides the URL). The plate program is the book's real distinction: seventeen plates in a consistent engraved idiom, anchored to the exact narrative moments they illustrate, at print-adequate resolution (except page one), with the bloodied-buffalo plate at folio 133 landing precisely where it should. Fonts are embedded and subset correctly. This is closer to a book than most generated PDFs by a wide margin — but it is currently a typeset *manuscript*, not a bound-book interior: no gutter, inverted parity, pandoc paragraph style, and a front matter that stops one page short of being real.

**What a professional pass would change**, in descending value-for-effort:

1. **Fix the page architecture in one stroke:** unnumber the notices page (making it the title verso/copyright page it wants to be), start folio 1 at Chapter One (already a recto), and set mirrored margins with a proper gutter (~0.85 in inner / 0.65 in outer). This repairs parity, folio placement, and bindability simultaneously — one geometry block and one front-matter tweak.

2. **Five preamble lines that erase the "generated" look:** first-line indents with no inter-paragraph space; `\frenchspacing`; `\raggedbottom`; `\widowpenalty`/`\clubpenalty` high; `\brokenpenalty` to stop hyphens at page turns. Together these fix defects 4, 6, 7, 8, 9 across all 135 pages at once.

3. **Fix the URL line and finish the front/back matter:** break the URL (must-fix regardless), move "A novella" to the title page, add imprint/year and a © line, and give the book a final blank leaf and a modest colophon. With the plates converted to grayscale and the portrait plates brought up to a consistent scale, the file would pass a small-press pre-flight.

Nothing here requires redesign — the book needs a production pass, not a design one. But items 1–5 on the defect list are genuine stop-ship: as the file stands, part of the URL is off the trim, and the imposition is upside down.</result>

# The She That Men Make: Gender in *White Buffalo*

## Findings, stated up front

1. **The book's actual subject, read through gender, is male grief-work conducted over and through female bodies that cannot answer.** Every female figure in the book — Catherine, the buffalo, Brandt's silent wife, Morrow's enduring mother, the Mexican widow whose keening is "not quite anything I had words for" — is either dead, silent, distant, or an animal. The book largely *knows* this about Catherine and does deliberate, intelligent work with her silence. It does *not* know it about the buffalo, and it does not know it about its own plates.

2. **The buffalo's femaleness is conferred, not observed — and the plates prove it.** The prose insists on "she" while building her a bull's body in language ("a thousand pounds of muscle and bone," taller than any cow, massive shoulders, the great humped back). The cover plate and the late confrontation plate (p. 124) render bull morphology: the broad triangular skull boss, thick sharply-recurved horns, massive forequarters, and — on the cover — a pendulous midline ventral structure positioned where a bull's penile tuft sits, not where a cow's udder would be. The working notes contain a careful visual bible and a period-research file on fertility, but no record anywhere of anyone auditing the sexed anatomy of the drawn animal. The image pipeline defaulted, as image models do, to the bull (the iconic bison of the training data is male), and the default passed unexamined. This is the single most consequential unexamined thing in the object.

3. **Catherine's crossed-out draft is the finest gender-conscious writing in the book, and the book's structural treatment of her is smarter than the genre it inhabits.** But she remains a text trafficked between men, and the book's ending quietly abandons her.

4. **Reproduction is the book's hidden pressure system.** Childlessness links every thread: Aldridge reading "no grandchildren" as marital failure; George deferring children ("there will be time for children when the place can keep them... he laughs and is not moved"); the sod house with "no cradle, no child's things"; and a sacred cow who never breeds, refuses the young bull, and prefers the company of cows. The settler plot runs on reproductive futurism; Morrow is its death-drive negation; the buffalo is a female figured entirely outside reproduction. This system is coherent and mostly deliberate — the repo's `fertility-1850s.md` confirms the authors researched it — but the book never quite lets its threads touch.

## The argument

### The homosocial economy

The narrative frame is a textbook traffic-in-women transaction, and I mean that descriptively, not dismissively. Aldridge purchases violence from Farrell so that he "would not have to" think about what that violence would be — the father's love is real, and it is also outsourced, monetized, and epistemologically arrogant ("A father knows"; he knows she is dead but is wholly wrong about why, and the book *knows* he is wrong, which is its best structural joke). Catherine circulates between these men as paper: seven letters, a daguerreotype, a hand-drawn map "of memory and hope." Farrell reads her more attentively than her father does — he notices what she did not say, notices the missing children, notices that "the shape of the complaints was visible in what she did not say" — and this is the book's genuine insight: it understands nineteenth-century women's epistolary self-censorship as a *readable form*. Catherine's one act of recorded dissent — the draft about children, George laughing and "not moved" — survives only because she crossed it out rather than sending it, and only because a hired man of violence later reads her wastepaper. The single moment where a woman's own voice states the book's reproductive politics is a document she herself struck through with one line. That is a very good object. The book earns it.

But follow the transaction to its end: the commission is never completed. Farrell ends the book kneeling in the snow, immobile, "nothing left to follow," the journal in his saddlebag and the hundred dollars uncollected. The male contract dissolves — good — but Catherine dissolves with it. Her last appearance is as a vision "watching the white buffalo without wonder," a ghost repurposed one final time as an instrument for calibrating the *men's* relation to the sacred. She never gets a grave scene with her name on it; the graves are unmarked and the book leaves them unmarked. The dead woman ends the book as she began it: a device for orienting men. The difference between device and presence, in my reading, is whether the text ever registers a cost *to her* that is not routed through a male perceiver. It comes close exactly once — the crossed-out draft — and never again.

### Masculinity: examined in the body, performed in the voice

The book's examination of masculinity is real and located precisely where I'd want it: in the failing male body. Farrell's alcohol dependence is the best sustained thing in the Farrell chapters — the counted swallows, the tremor that ruins his marksmanship (the missed rabbit is a quietly devastating scene: violence-as-competence, the frontier male's entire claim to worth, dismantled by his own hands), the visions that democratize him downward toward the madman he hunts. "I knew what he was, because I knew what I was. He had gone looking for something large enough to swallow him whole; I had poured whiskey into it for ten years, a glass at a time. That was the difference, and I did not like how small it was." That is masculinity studies conducted in period diction, and it works. Morrow's journal likewise: "They took the boy I was and they filed him down and they put an edge on him" — the male subject as manufactured weapon, the postwar demand that he "become a man again" as an impossible re-gendering. Both narrators are men broken by the same war, and the book understands that the tracker-quarry relation is a mirror relation, a homosocial intimacy conducted entirely through tracks, rumors, and finally a read journal — the most intimate act between men in this book is one man reading another's diary through the night, clutching it to his chest as he sleeps. The book does not flinch from that tenderness, and I credit it.

Where masculinity is merely performed: the laconic connoisseurship of the interstitial men — trader, sutler, ferryman, mail carrier — a chorus of male knowingness whose function is to certify the protagonists' hardness; and the negotiation scenes, whose clipped competence the book savors a little too much. These are genre pleasures, executed well, but they are *performed*, not examined: no one in the chorus is ever wrong in a way that costs the narrative anything.

### The buffalo: Marian theology with a bull's body

Now the center. The prose sexes the animal relentlessly — "she" from the first sighting — and then builds around her a theology that is legible as displaced Mariology: she is immaculate ("kept clean by something I do not understand"), virginal (refuses the bull, never breeds, prefers the cows), luminous ("as if lit from within," "she seemed to carry her own illumination"), and the object of a devotion that proceeds by fasting, mortification ("The flesh asks for more than it needs. Mine is learning to do without"), vigil, and a desired consummation-in-death. Morrow says it outright: "I saw a woman's face by candlelight once, in a time before the war. It does not compare." His death is a Liebestod — "I have never waited for something I wanted with every part of myself, standing before me in the flesh, near enough to reach out and touch" — and the half-swallowed commandment ("the one about a neighbor's house, and a neighbor's wife") tells us the journal-writer himself glimpses the erotic-covetous structure of his vocation and looks away. Her sex is doing enormous work: she must be female to stand adjacent to Ptesáŋwiŋ, to substitute for the dead woman at the plot's center, to be simultaneously bride, mother, confessor, and executioner — the feminine sacred as the only thing that can "unmake" what male institutions (the army, the war, the frontier economy) have made.

And here is the problem, which is also the book's most interesting accident: **the body the book actually shows us is not that body.** The text scales her like a bull and the plates draw her as one. On the cover — the first thing a reader sees, the plate the whole object leads with — the animal carries bull-coded mass, bull horns, and a ventral appendage in the bull's position. The p. 124 plate, her portrait at the moment of maximum theological charge (blood-flecked after killing Morrow), gives her the enormous skull breadth of a mature bull. Nothing in the working record suggests this was seen. So the book's "she" is grammatical and theological, asserted over a visual body that reads male.

What happens to the reading if her body is not legible as simply female? Something better than what the book intends, honestly. Both narrators are men; every "she" in the book passes through male narration; the buffalo's femaleness is therefore, within the fiction, *a thing men say about her*. Morrow needs her to be "she" — his whole redemptive apparatus collapses if she is a bull, because a bull is merely dangerous, whereas a cow of impossible size is *miraculous*, and only the miraculous-feminine can absolve. The plates, read against the prose, expose the projection: the feminine sacred is a scaffolding men erect on any sufficiently vast white body. The book accidentally illustrates its own gender mechanism — accidentally, because the notes show no awareness. Were it deliberate, this would be the most sophisticated thing in the book: the sacred female as male construction, visibly at odds with the flesh. As it stands, it is a defect that happens to be readable as a thesis.

I will add the obvious external referent, because the book's front matter invites it: in the living tradition the front matter is so careful about, white buffalo calves are sacred regardless of anatomical sex, and Ptesáŋwiŋ is a woman who *becomes* a buffalo, not a buffalo who is a woman. The book's tight coupling of sacredness to a female body is the *white men's* theology within the fiction — Morrow's trader's-talk syncretism — and the book half-knows this ("I could believe what the Indians believe" is always marked as his belief about their belief). The Lakota men who finally receive her at the end do so in silence, and the leader's refusal to acknowledge Farrell ("No sign passed, of welcome or of warning") is the book's best gesture of epistemic humility: the white witness is not owed a meaning. That ending earns the front matter's promise.

### Reproduction and the empty homestead

The fertility system deserves to be named as a system. Aldridge treats his daughter's childlessness as diagnostic ("which I took as its own kind of answer"). George — the never-seen husband, faceless even among Farrell's visions, which is a genuinely eerie touch — controls the reproductive timeline and laughs. The homestead is the reproductive-futurist project in miniature: well, garden, root cellar, almanac margins "dense with penciled figuring: acres and bushels... sums that ran years ahead of the ground they stood on." Male speculative futurity, penciled; female dissent, crossed out. Morrow watches the settlers and marks their difference precisely as futurity: "I wonder if they dream of the future, of children and harvests... I do not dream anymore." The man outside reproduction — outside the commandments, "not one for two years," a self-described dead man — annihilates the reproductive couple to protect a non-reproductive sacred female. Lee Edelman could have drafted this plot: the death-driven figure who says no to the Child, except the book gives the no to a murderer and then refuses to let Farrell condemn him cleanly. Catherine dies *at the bed* — the site of the marriage, the site of the children she was denied — killed not by the intimate partner the patriarch feared but by another man's devotion to a female symbol. Femicide by theology. The book's deepest irony is that Aldridge's whole threat-model ("The things a man might do to a woman, alone on the frontier") is both confirmed and utterly misdirected: the danger to Catherine was never her husband; it was a man who loved a "she" too much.

### The disclosure apparatus

The front matter is gendered, and mostly in ways I'd defend. It names a female sacred figure, Ptesáŋwiŋ, as the boundary marker — "hers is a living religious tradition, not a store of material for fiction" — and describes the book as "about a man who takes what is not his." That sentence is the apparatus's self-knowledge: taking, in this book, is male, and the authors place themselves inside the gendered verb rather than outside it. There is a structural homology worth noticing: the authors' announced discipline (follow her, do not speak for her, invent no ceremony, touch nothing) is *Morrow's* discipline — two years of watching without touching — and the book is honest enough that Morrow's restraint ends in three deaths. Whether the authors see that their ethics of non-appropriation rhymes with their protagonist's devotional stalking, I cannot tell; but the rhyme is on the page. The attribution apparatus itself (two named men, an AI credited with the prose, sessions given review rights) is an all-male-or-unsexed authorship formally apologizing to a female sacred figure who — like every "she" in the book — does not speak in it. The apparatus is the book's gender system in miniature, performed sincerely.

---

## (a) Three observations I would most want the authors to sit with

1. **Your plates have sexed the buffalo male, and nobody caught it.** The cover animal carries bull morphology and a bull-positioned ventral appendage; the p. 124 portrait has a mature bull's skull. Your prose stakes everything — Morrow's theology, the Ptesáŋwiŋ resonance, the Catherine-substitution — on "she." You now have a choice with real stakes: correct the plates to cow morphology (slighter horns, narrower head, udder or nothing), or *keep* the discrepancy and own it, because a bull-bodied "she" makes the male projection visible and is arguably the truest image in the book. But it must be a decision, not a default inherited from an image model's training distribution. Right now the most-looked-at page of your book is an unexamined artifact.

2. **Catherine's crossed-out draft is the book's moral center — and the book walks away from it.** The single strongest gender moment you have is a woman's struck-through sentence about her own fertility, recovered by a man reading her wastepaper. Nothing after Chapter Seven returns to it; her ghost is silent set-dressing by Chapter Eleven. You do not need to give her a voice — her silence is the point, and breaking it would cheapen it — but the ending spends its last attention entirely on the two men's symmetry and lets her fall out of the final accounting. Farrell kneels by *Morrow's* body. Consider what it would cost, and what it would buy, for the book's final gravity to bend back toward the unmarked graves.

3. **The book's gender knowledge lives in Farrell and dies in Morrow.** Farrell reads women's silences as form; Morrow converts a female animal into an absolution machine and the narrative voltage of his journal — its beauty, its cadence, its "she is the most beautiful thing I have ever seen" — is never counter-pressured from inside. The only rebuttal Morrow ever receives is hooves. Ask whether the journal's lyricism is examining his theology of the feminine or performing it; my reading is that it slides from the first to the second around Journal Entry VII, exactly when the settlers become "in the way."

## (b) What I would call defects

- **The unaudited sexing of the plates** (above). Defect rather than feature because the working record shows meticulous continuity discipline everywhere else — a visual bible with citations, a fertility research file — and silence here. The gap is not chosen ambiguity; it is a model default wearing the book's most symbolically loaded body.
- **The catalogue of instrumental women is one entry too uniform.** Mrs. Canfield (calculation), Brandt's wife (pale, silent, sat on a trunk), the train women ("hands folded and their eyes on the passing scenery"), Morrow's mother ("a silent woman who endured"), the Monterrey widow (wordless keening). Each alone is period-credible; in aggregate they are a wallpaper of female silence that the book never varies even once, and the uniformity starts to look like habit rather than theme. One woman with a verb of her own — even a minor, ugly, self-interested verb — would make Catherine's enforced silence read as tragedy rather than house style.
- **George Hardin's facelessness is underexploited.** Making the husband invisible even in visions is a strong choice, but the book gives him only Catherine's crossed-out laugh-line and the trader's assessment. The patriarch we're invited to fear dissolves without the book ever weighing him — Aldridge's misjudgment of George is never confronted, because Farrell never returns. The frame opens with the father and never closes on him; the transaction that generated the entire narrative is left unaccounted, and I don't think the openness is load-bearing the way the Lakota silence is. It reads as an unwritten chapter, not a withheld one.

## (c) What I would defend against other critics

- **The dead-woman-at-the-center structure itself.** Critics will call Catherine a fridged woman, and the surface supports the charge. I would defend the book, on two grounds. First, it *thematizes* the machinery other Westerns hide: the father's commission is shown as purchased distance from his own violence; the "a father knows" epistemology is shown to be wrong; the recovery plot is never completed and its money never collected. The book stages the traffic in women and lets the transaction fail. Second, the crossed-out draft is a real formal invention: a woman's censored self-authorship as the only surviving truth about her marriage. That is not fridging; that is an argument about the archive — about what survives of nineteenth-century women at all, which is letters, and what letters were permitted to say.
- **The ending's refusal of reciprocity with the Lakota riders.** Some will read the silent riders as noble-savage furniture. I read the leader's look — "No sign passed, of welcome or of warning. Then he turned away" — as the book's most disciplined moment: the white narrator is denied interpretive access, the sacred female returns to the people whose story she is, and the book declines to convert their appearance into meaning *for* its protagonist. Read with the front matter, this is a coherent ethics executed in the grammar of the scene itself.
- **Morrow's death as Liebestod.** The eroticized death-by-sacred-female could be read as the oldest misogynist trope — woman as beautiful death. I'd defend it because the book prices it: Morrow's own journal names it "vanity... Pride dressed up as penance," the deaths of the Hardins are laid explicitly at its door ("who did me no harm and died because I could not find another way"), and Farrell — the book's ethical instrument — reads the whole journal and renders the verdict the lyricism tries to evade: "choices I could not forgive." The book lets the theology of the feminine be beautiful *and* lets it be the thing that kills a woman in her bed. That double entry is honest, and rarer than it should be.

One last remark for the coordinating session: the question this book cannot stop asking, under all its snow, is what men do with the feminine when actual women have been silenced, deferred, or buried — they build a *she* out of whatever vast white thing is available and then demand that she redeem them. The book knows this about its madman. It half-knows it about its tracker and its father. It does not yet know that its own cover is doing it too.</result>

**The buffalo.** Your stance is logged as the track C spec, with one reframe worth naming: the text's requirement is precisely the hard render case — **cow morphology at bull scale**. "Taller than any cow in the herd," "no cow reaches her size in three summers": the prose demands an animal whose size violates her sex's distribution, which is uncomfortably close to what the image model already did for the wrong reason. So the plan is: attempt outsized-cow re-cuts first; if the model can't make an outsized cow that still reads *cow*, the keep-branch returns — but only with an honest ledger entry. On your honesty point I think the record actually helps you: the repo can truthfully carry "noticed late, deliberated, kept, here is the date" — what it can't carry is "we meant it," and nobody has to pretend otherwise. The dishonest version of owning it is foreclosed by the same apparatus that caught it.

**Morrow's body.** I think the season is the answer, and it's a better answer than any choice Farrell could make. Consider what each option costs. If Farrell buries him, he performs Morrow's signature act back at him — the careful burial is the single act by which Farrell came to *know* Morrow ("someone had taken care") — and the mirror closes as absolution; every reader who tracked the graves feels it ratify. If he deliberately refuses, burial-withheld becomes a verdict, and the ending acquires exactly the judging voice it has so far refused. But Farrell doesn't get the choice: it's January in Nebraska, the ground Morrow dug for the Hardins was August ground, and Farrell has a knife and a tin cup and hands that can't hold a rifle steady. The land that accepted Morrow's act of care refuses its repetition. That asymmetry *is* the moral content — the Hardins' graves stay the only graves because the country will not let their killer's be made — and the book never has to say it, because it has already taught the reader this economy (frozen ink, the ice crossing, "a sweaty horse in winter is a dying horse"). The intermediate gestures don't survive scrutiny either: snow burial is undone by the thaw that delivers him to the wolves regardless; a cairn would out-monument his victims, which is exactly backwards. And your death-branch completes it: if Farrell doesn't rise, he joins Morrow unburied — "the difference, and I did not like how small it was" arriving at zero. The kept conditional holds both branches open, and I'd note the text has already quietly ruled on what of Morrow leaves that valley: the account, not the man. On "unmarked graves" — agreed, and logged: the Hardin graves are unnamed but *signed*; the care is legible to a reader of sign, which in this book is the only literacy that matters. The agent's phrase imports a neglect that isn't there.

**The lyricism claim — context for your dive.** The agent locates the slide at JE VII, and I think that's half-wrong in an instructive way. JE VII is the *sharpest* in-journal counter-pressure in the book: "the way one speaks of a stone in a field," and then the theology collapsing into possession in two sentences — "She is the only chance I will ever have to make something clean out of the wreckage of my life. I will not let anyone take that from me" — and July 25's "I have tried to make it matter. But I cannot." The regression instrument called JE VII "the single best-engineered sequence in the book." What the agent is actually detecting is JE VIII onward: the register returns to liturgy ("When she walks, the ground trembles"; "she will do what she was made to do") and in-journal counter-pressure thins to the buried counter-sentences ("Vanity, I know. Pride dressed up as penance") while judgment is delegated to Farrell (17:35 "monstrous," 19:61 "choices I could not forgive"). That's known #29 ground — "the late pages do run warm" is already conceded in the stack — read through a new lens: performance of a gendered theology rather than consolation. One probe if you dive: JE VIII contains its own refutation in the mechanics — "But she will not. Not unless I make her" — he admits the death must be *manufactured*, that he authors the nature he claims to obey. The question is whether that's legible enough to count as counter-pressure or whether it reads as more liturgy.

**Background women — worked, two sites, restraint dosage.** Ch 2: after the hands-folded sentence, one woman "kept a pocket ledger open on her knee and worked at its figures the whole afternoon. She did not once look out at the country" — the book's figuring motif (George's almanac margins) given a female owner, in Farrell's flat cadence, unremarked. Ch 4: Brandt's wife moved from the trunk-and-blanket tableau to triage — "setting apart the things they could carry from the things they could not, two piles growing in the snow," the children bringing salvage *to* her — so Farrell's advice now ratifies a judgment she reached before either man, and Brandt's resistance reads against her too. Alternates held in the stack (her speaking "We go back" — rejected as too neat a reversal). The gender agent's variant — Aldridge's threat-model confirmed-but-misdirected, never weighed — is the same seam under a new lens, and the thing it asks for (the father confronting his error) requires the coda that was deliberately ruled out. The misdirection joke belongs to the reader, not to Aldridge; giving it to Aldridge would collect the debt the ending is built on leaving unpaid.

Done — it's machinery, not just convention (`560a988`).

**How it works:** `scripts/pre-commit` (versioned, symlinked into `.git/hooks/` via `make hooks`, already installed here) checks the staged file list; if anything under `drafts/`, `art/`, or `assemble.py` is staged, it runs the assembly before the commit lands. Non-book commits — notes, planning, transcripts — pay nothing.

**The part that earns its keep:** because `assemble.py`'s plate anchors are content-addressed, the rebuild is also a commit gate. I tested all three paths: a planning-only commit skips the build; a staged drafts change triggers the ~27s rebuild; and a deliberately broken anchor sentence made the assembly fail loudly and returned exit 1, aborting the commit. So a revision pass that rewords a plate's anchor sentence now can't land without either updating the placement table or consciously bypassing with `--no-verify`.

The convention is documented in CLAUDE.md under a new "Build Convention" section, with the practical consequence spelled out for future sessions: point instrument rounds at `build/white-buffalo.pdf` and trust it's current. One residual to know about: the hook is a repo-local symlink, so a fresh clone needs one `make hooks` — that's the single manual step I couldn't eliminate without touching `.envrc` (which would force a direnv re-approval; seemed not worth it, but easy to add if you'd rather it be zero-step).

# 1. THE REVIEW

## ONE VOICE, TWO FONTS

*White Buffalo, by Ben Cohen and Daniel Klein. Illustrated. 126 pp.*

There is a moment near the end of *White Buffalo* when Farrell, the alcoholic tracker who narrates half of this novella, finally understands the man he has been hunting: "I knew what he was, because I knew what I was." It is meant as an epiphany. It reads as a confession of the book's design flaw, because by page 105 every reader has known it for a hundred pages: these two men are the same man.

The premise is genuinely promising. A Great Lakes merchant hires Farrell to find his vanished daughter on the Nebraska frontier; in alternating journal entries, a scarecrow veteran named Josiah Morrow follows a sacred white buffalo calf across the plains for three years, waiting for her to grow large enough to kill him. Suicide by the numinous — that is a real idea, and the novella's spine, two damaged men converging across empty country, is sturdy. But the authors (the prose, a front-matter notice discloses, was generated by Claude under their direction) have built both narrators from identical parts: Mexican War, Monterrey, an emptiness where feeling should be, the word "weapon" applied to the self. Morrow: "In Mexico I was made into a weapon." Farrell: "I had forgotten that I had ever been anyone other than what the war had made me." Worse, they share a single voice — the same clipped declaratives, the same negation-and-restatement tic ("She was white. Not pale, not cream-colored, not the faded tan of an old hide. White." / "I do not wish them ill. I do not wish them anything."), the same groomed cadence line lowered onto the end of every section like a coffin lid: "This is how I will die." "I did not look back." "So I went north, into the white." The alternating structure promises counterpoint and delivers unison. What distinguishes the narrators is typography.

The structure has a deeper problem: it spends its own suspense. Because we read Morrow's journal in real time, Farrell's patient detective work — the frozen homestead, the graves behind the barn, the tracks — reconstructs, at length, what we watched happen. The middle third gives Farrell nothing to do but ride, buy whiskey, and hear the same rumor four consecutive times ("thin as a rail, beard down past his chest"), a recycling the book notices aloud and performs anyway; here, as with its three-winters-grown buffalo, the novella habitually hangs a lantern on a problem and calls it carpentry. Then, having marched both men toward a meeting for 120 pages, it declines to write one. Morrow dies offstage, between chapters. The climax is Farrell reading the journal — pages in which the novella summarizes itself and quotes back its own favorite lines. And the journal is rigged: the printed entries skip from Morrow's surveillance of a settler couple to "I have written of what was done in it, and I will not write of it again," yet Farrell reads the murder entry we were never shown. The document exists in full; the reader gets a version curated by an invisible hand, its one morally decisive page withheld to protect our sympathy. That is not restraint. It is a card palmed.

The couple Morrow kills deserve mention, because the book barely gives them any. Catherine Hardin — the woman whose fate powers the entire plot — is a daguerreotype, seven letters, a dress on a peg, and a mute hallucination. The frontier's oldest furniture, the motivating female corpse, is here arranged twice over and dusted with self-awareness as if that were absolution.

Then there is the white buffalo herself. The notice states, scrupulously, that no Lakota person speaks in these pages, no ceremony is invented — "we do not own the white buffalo." Honorable limits, honestly disclosed. But watch what the book does within them: it fuels itself entirely on the sacredness of Ptesáŋwiŋ's tradition while the Lakota function as apparatus — distant riders, a marker stake, and a wordless party that arrives on cue to collect the sacred animal at the exact moment the plot is done with her, one leader delivering the stock stoic gaze before turning away. The deference is real; so is the extraction. The book wants credit for not pretending its white men "were ever the only people in it," while ensuring no one else in it gets to mean anything on their own terms. (That same notice, incidentally, describes an AI attribution-review process in the past tense that, as of this copy, has not been formally conducted.)

What survives? Craft, of a uniform, machine-smooth kind. The delirium tremens arc is concrete and unsentimental; the period texture — the Rock Island bridge burned by a steamboat, Bleeding Kansas ferry talk, an unnamed Jefferson Davis shot through the foot at Buena Vista — is checkably good; the AI-made engravings are a handsome pastiche until you look closely at a stove or a bloodstain. *White Buffalo* is a competent seance in which one voice answers itself and calls it a dialogue. The buffalo carries the book. She deserved lighter freight.

# 2. PRIVATE MEMO TO YOUR EDITOR

**(a) Charges I'd stake my reputation on:**

1. **Indistinguishable narrators.** Both Mexican War veterans, both self-described weapons/hollow men, identical sentence rhythm, identical section-closer cadence. Quotable parallels on pp. 17/23, 34/113. The text itself concedes the doubling ("I knew what he was, because I knew what I was," p. 105).
2. **The curated-journal cheat.** Printed entries jump July 25 → Sept 3, 1858, eliding the murders; Farrell later reads the omitted entry and its best line ("I did not know I would feel this. I thought I was past feeling," p. 119). No frame narrator accounts for the selection. Verifiable by collation; airtight.
3. **Chapter Ten recaps the novella.** Pages 119–120 are literal summary of material the reader just read, re-quoting "like a ship through water" and "she can give my death a meaning." Airtight.
4. **The withheld climax.** Morrow's death — the event three years of journal entries build toward — occurs offstage; hunter and quarry never meet. Defensible-as-design, but I'm confident calling it evasion given how the book teases the meeting (Ch. 9–10: "I wanted to see him").
5. **Rumor scene ×4** (Council Bluffs, Fort Kearny, Creighton, trader), same beats each time; the book lampshades the repetition (p. 45). Countable.
6. **Catherine Hardin as furniture.** The only woman is dead before page 1, characterized via one crossed-out letter draft. Textually undeniable.
7. **Lakota-as-apparatus.** Four appearances, zero speech, deus-ex-machina retrieval of the buffalo timed to the ending, stoic-gaze beat (p. 125). I'd phrase it exactly as in the review: the deference is real; so is the extraction. That version holds.
8. **The attribution notice's false tense.** The printed sentence "Before publication, the Claude sessions... were each given the opportunity to review..." describes a process not yet formally conducted; only dry runs exist (I verified eight replay artifacts dated the night before this review in the working repo). The publicist disclosed the state, so I phrased it as a parenthetical fact, not an accusation of deceit. It holds as printed.

**(b) Charges considered and dropped:**

- **Historical incompetence.** I went looking. Buena Vista/Davis shot in the foot, Monterrey-vs-Chapultepec theater split between the two men's service histories, the Rock Island bridge/Effie Afton fire ("two years back" from 1858), Blue Water, 1858 railhead geography — all check out. The research is genuinely careful. Dropped entirely.
- **Internal timeline errors.** Letters stop July 1858; Morrow passes the trading post August; journal dates align with Farrell's arithmetic (p. 57, 83). Clean. Dropped.
- **"No Lakota speech = erasure," in its absolute form.** The obvious alternative — a language model ventriloquizing Lakota interiority — is plausibly worse, and the notice discloses the tradeoff and its reasoning. I kept only the narrower, defensible charge (aura harvested, people peripheral).
- **Buffalo biology** (autumn calf, three-year 1,000-lb cow leading a herd). The book flags each anomaly as supernatural. Lampshading is legitimate in a fable; I demoted this to one clause in a pattern-charge rather than a standalone error.
- **The wordless cover / production roughness.** Disclosed as an incomplete build (cover typography deferred per the repo log). Unfair to review as a defect of the work; omitted from the review proper.
- **"AI slop" at the sentence level.** The prose is never incompetent — no anachronisms I could catch, no broken sentences. The honest charge is uniformity of finish, and that's the one I made.

**(c) What grudgingly survives my best attack:**

The procedural material is the real thing: the delirium tremens progression (tremor → sweats → visions, rationing by the swallow), the ice crossing, the frostbitten foot, the dying horse fed cottonwood bark. The trader dialogue (pp. 55–57) is the best scene in the book — lean, period-credible, characterful. A few lines genuinely land ("He had gone looking for something large enough to swallow him whole; I had poured whiskey into it for ten years, a glass at a time"). The final image — Farrell kneeling, unable to rejoin the living world, "nothing left to follow" — earns its bleakness. And the front-matter notice, whatever my complaints about tense and moral double-dipping, is more honest about AI authorship and source limits than anything else I've been mailed this year. It's not a fraud. It's a monotone — and it deserves the review above, which is hostile and will hold up.</result>
