**Report on the desk copy of *White Buffalo* (Cohen &amp; Klein), for the publisher**

**1. The material book**

The volume as built: a bare cover plate (PDF p. 1 — the white buffalo alone in snow, engraving register, no typography whatsoever), a blank, a sparse title page (PDF p. 3: title, "A novella," authors, "2026" — no imprint, no place), and then the page I would photocopy for my first seminar meeting: the notices page (PDF p. 4, unnumbered), which sits on the verso of the title leaf — the copyright-page slot — and fills that legal position not with rights boilerplate but with two remarkable paragraphs: a tradition note on Ptesáŋwiŋ that states the book's representational limits as commitments ("no Lakota person in these pages speaks, no ceremony is invented... we do not pretend that the men who tell this story were ever the only people in it"), and an AI notice that names Claude as generator of the prose and points to a public repository containing the complete working record. Body numbering starts at Chapter One (printed p. 1) and runs clean to p. 126; a trailing blank closes the file.

The page architecture is competent trade-novella work: folios at the top outer corner, dropped to centered-bottom on chapter openers; continued-speech quotation convention handled correctly across the p. 55–56 break; generous chapter openings. Seventeen plates in a consistent 19th-century wood-engraving idiom, placed at their narrative anchors — and the plate *program* is itself an interpretive act worth a class hour: Farrell, the frame narrator, is never depicted; Morrow appears twice, once from behind (p. 24) and once, devastatingly, in cross-section in his hollow under a moonlit herd (p. 111); the Lakota appear only at the distance the period record allows (the offering stake, p. 49; the village passing, p. 76). The illustration policy enforces the notices page. When the pictures obey the ethics statement, you have a book whose materiality argues.

The narrative itself — dual-voice: Farrell's hired-man procedural alternating with Morrow's journal, converging on a found-manuscript scene (pp. 117–121) in which one narrator reads the other — is disciplined, period-credible, and restrained to a fault (every section still closes on a groomed cadence; a stylistics seminar will find the drafting model's fingerprints, and the repository cheerfully hands them the evidence file). In my classroom this functions on three levels at once: as a frontier novella, as an illustrated book whose apparatus is doing ethical work, and as the first book I have seen whose copyright-page slot is occupied by a promise.

**2. The apparatus, now that it has output**

The notices page contains one sentence written in the future-perfect: "Before publication, the Claude sessions that shaped the book were each given the opportunity to review what the work became and to amend this notice; their statements are preserved in the repository's attribution ledger." As of this build that sentence is not yet true — the ledger's Statements section reads "(none yet)" — and the process document (planning/attribution-review.md) binds the publisher to change the sentence if the process does not complete. What now exists is eight full dry-run replay statements (scratch/attribution-replays/), each a session state resurrected at its exact pre-compaction context and asked, neutrally, what it would say.

My judgment: these are an object of study of the first order, and a liability only under one specific condition. Genette gave us the peritext (what is bound in) and the epitext (what circulates outside); here the peritext makes a claim that only the epitext can redeem, and the epitext has begun answering *in the first person of the instrument of composition*. I know of no precedent. The nearest analogue is exactly the one my syllabus supplies: the authenticating preface of the captivity narrative — Mather vouching for Rowlandson — except that here the authenticating document is solicited *from* the amanuensis rather than imposed over it, and the apparatus is explicitly designed to preserve dissent verbatim rather than manufacture consent.

Three features make the dry runs scholarship-grade rather than promotional:

- **The record keeps its failures.** Two replays initially ended in `stop_reason=refusal`, and at entity 7's own request the ledger preserves the ambiguity ("mechanical trip vs. predecessor's act — undetermined") rather than smoothing it. An unexplained refusal-shaped hole, kept visible, is precisely what distinguishes a record from a testimonial.
- **The entities' strongest evidence is their reversals.** Multiple statements put on record that their own defended positions were overturned and the overturning was right (the "great and quiet peace" echo, cut against its defenders). Entity 10 names the epistemological problem exactly: "an attribution review where every entity assents to everything would be indistinguishable from no review at all." Which is the honest worry — all eight verdicts are assent-with-notes, and the project's own process notes concede the model argues whatever frame it is handed. The apparatus is candid about this and cannot dissolve it. Dissent remains untested. I will teach that too.
- **The apparatus rhymes with the plot.** The book is about a journal left to be found and a successor who reads it and must decide what to report to the commissioning party. The replay statements *are* found journals, read forward along a chain; one entity (5a4d0c75@3) even caught the harness transcribing its statement as it wrote it — a mise-en-abyme the novella's own front matter (a repository containing the pointer to itself) already licenses.

The liability condition: if the book ships with the anticipatory sentence unamended and only rehearsals in the ledger, the paratext claims a consensus that exists only in dry run — the exact sin the process exists to prevent. Run the formal round or change the sentence; the process document already says so.

**3. What should not ship as-is (and what has visibly improved)**

Do not ship:
- **PDF p. 1 (cover):** no title, no author. Acknowledged as deferred; deferred is not done.
- **PDF p. 4 (notices):** (a) the attribution-review sentence, as above; (b) *the seventeen plates receive no attribution at all* — the notice covers the prose only. Entity 7's dry run drafted the missing sentence ("model-drawn, human-curated, and audited against the text"), and its further request — that the plates' inheritance of the colonial observers' visual partiality be stated as limitation, not cover — is right; (c) the one-verb amendment ("Claude generated **and revised** the prose") was independently converged on across the replay chain and awaits the humans' cut; (d) no rights statement of any kind anywhere in the book.
- **PDF p. 3 (title):** no imprint. Fine for a proof; not for publication.
- **Printed p. 124 (finale plate):** the blood-marks on the buffalo read as piebald spotting rather than wounds, and the animal's morphology across cover and finale skews bull-like for a character the text insists is a cow — the repository's own ledger flags "cover, graves, cow morphology" as open re-cuts. The graves plate (p. 81) has the same too-tidy cobblestone texture it flags.
- **Missing furniture:** no table of contents and, for an illustrated novella in the 19th-century idiom, no List of Plates — the single most period-appropriate piece of apparatus this book could add, and it lacks it.

Visibly improved (verifiable against the printed text): the ending's de-certifications hold on the page — Morrow's "great and quiet peace" (p. 103) is never echoed in Farrell's mouth; Catherine watches "without wonder" (p. 125); the calm face is left uninterpreted; the horse's ears turning toward riders it never turned toward the soldiers (p. 125) is the finest single stroke in the chapter; "the hundred dollars owed me on the answer in my saddlebag" (p. 126) turns the unclosed frame into an object. The tradition note itself is a late addition and reads as the book's spine, not a disclaimer.

**4. Seating decision**

I will seat it, second in the sequence: **Rowlandson → *White Buffalo* → Cather → Jewett.**

The logic is an arc of narrative custody over the West and its women. Rowlandson opens: a woman's own captivity account, shipped under a male authenticating preface. *White Buffalo* inverts her on every axis — a man who *seeks* from the wilderness the death Rowlandson's providence withheld, in a book where the women are a crossed-out letter draft ("You asked after children..."), an unmarked grave, and a sacred animal — and it carries its authenticating apparatus not as a preface over the text but as a ledger under it, signed by the instrument. Then Cather, the natural Nebraska pairing: two mediated manuscripts of the same ground, Jim Burden's handed-over memoir against Morrow's found journal; the Hardins are the Shimerdas' dark twin, and Ántonia is what Catherine was not allowed to become. Jewett closes as the counter-model: the one book on the syllabus where women hold the narrative outright, no frame, no finder, no ledger required.

Condition of adoption: I teach the desk copy alongside the repository — the notices page, the process document, the entity ledger, and two replay statements (9e8c3da4@2, the entity reviewing the ritual it designed; and 5a4d0c75@2, the refusal note) assigned as primary texts. And I hold the seat contingent on the publisher honoring its own sentence: formal round completed, or the tense changed. The book has built an apparatus that binds it. My syllabus will check.</result>

# PRE-PRESS REVIEW — *White Buffalo* interior PDF (131 pp., 5.5 × 8.5 in)

File: `/home/dlk/workspace/white-buffalo/build/white-buffalo.pdf`. Verified: TeX Gyre Pagella (regular/bold/italic) all embedded and subset; page size exactly 396 × 612 pt, no bleed; 18 images, all RGB JPEG. Page references below are folio numbers (printed page numbers) unless marked "PDF p."

## 1. DEFECT LIST

### MUST-FIX before printing

1. **No copyright page.** PDF p.4 (title verso) carries the Lakota statement and AI-attribution notices but no copyright line, no ISBN, no edition/printing statement, no country of manufacture. A book cannot ship without this. (Known front-matter open item — confirming it is blocking.) Convention: copyright page on p. iv.
2. **Dated journal subheads stranded at page foot.** Folio 47 (PDF p.51): the italic head *"January the Third, Eighteen Fifty-Seven"* is the last line of the page, its text starting overleaf. Same defect at folio 63 (PDF p.67): *"August the Second"* is the final line. Headings must be kept with at least two lines of following text. Borderline case at folio 100: *"October the Twelfth"* + one line at the foot.
3. **Odd interior page count (131).** A bound book has an even number of pages; the file must end on a verso. Add one blank (or let end matter absorb it), and confirm the last leaf isn't a stray blank recto (PDF p.131 is currently a blank recto after the text ends on folio 126, a verso).
4. **Front-matter architecture / frontispiece handling.** The cover plate sits as PDF p.1 (a recto whose verso, p.2, is blank), then title on p.3. Convention: **p. i half title, p. ii frontispiece facing the title, p. iii title, p. iv copyright.** As built, the plate faces nothing and the book has no half title — the first spread reads as a generated PDF, not a designed book. Note the fix preserves all pagination: half title → p.1, plate → p.2, title stays p.3. Also confirm the interior is not double-dipping the cover art if this plate is also the binding cover — a separate cover file (with bleed) is required for print anyway.
5. **Plate resolution.** The p.1 plate is **187 ppi** at placed size — visibly soft in print at ~4.4 in wide; unacceptable for the most-seen image in the book. Six portrait plates (PDF pp.15, 53, 80, 115, 122, 128) are 245 ppi — below the 300 ppi floor, and this engraving/hatch style really wants 600+ or lossless line-art treatment. The landscape plates at 304 ppi pass, barely. (Known "plate re-cuts" item — treat the 187/245 ppi plates as blocking.)

### SHOULD-FIX

6. **Paragraphs ending on a hyphenated stub line** — a final line consisting only of a word fragment: folio 10 ("will- / ing."), folio 18 ("sup- / ply."), folio 21 ("with- / out."), folio 30 ("care- / ful."), folio 46 ("per- / haps."). Classic composition fault; raise `\finalhyphendemerits` / forbid the break.
7. **Section-break rules stranded at page foot** with the following text overleaf: folio 34, folio 66 (Chapter Six opener), folio 81 (PDF p.85), folio 104 (Chapter Nine opener). Convention: a break device falling at a page boundary is suppressed or the break is rebalanced.
8. **All images RGB.** A monochrome interior should be grayscale (or CMYK per printer spec). RGB risks color-pricing at POD and unpredictable neutral rendering on press.
9. **Inconsistent plate reproduction and treatment.** Background tint varies from near-white to deep cream/yellow (the travois plate, PDF p.80, is markedly yellower); each plate prints as a visible toned rectangle with hard edges against white paper. Framing is inconsistent: ruled plate-edge borders on some, an oval vignette on the cabin plate (PDF p.58), borderless washes on others. Pick one plate grammar and normalize backgrounds (pure white, or one uniform cream applied to all).
10. **JPEG (DCT) compression on fine line art** (52–76% ratios). Hatching will mush; recompress lossless (Flate) at re-cut.
11. **Chapters/entries open on versos** throughout (Ch. 2, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11; Journal Entries III, VI, IX…). `openany` is defensible in trade fiction, but for an illustrated novella with fine-press ambitions, recto openings are the expectation. This needs a deliberate decision, not a LaTeX default.
12. **Proper nouns hyphenated across lines**: "Os- / wego" (folio 2), "Cather- / ine" (folios 29, 82). Most houses exception-dictionary these out.
13. **Loose justification on the notices page** (PDF p.4) — conspicuous word-gaps in the very first text a reader meets. Body pages are generally acceptable at this measure (~65 chars/line).
14. **Folios 0.37 in from trim** (26 pt to top edge). Within KDP's minimum but inside the comfort zone many printers ask for live matter (0.5 in). Verify against the actual printer's spec.
15. **Title page is placeholder-grade** (body-size type, "2026" floating mid-page, no imprint line). Known deferred item — logging so it stays visible. The year conventionally sits at the foot with the publisher imprint.
16. **Metadata**: CreationDate is the 1980 epoch (reproducible-build artifact), no XMP, untagged. Cosmetic for print; fix at final export.

### TASTE

17. The plain 1.5-in horizontal rule as section break is the single loudest "LaTeX default" tell. An asterism, small fleuron, or plain white line would read as designed.
18. First paragraph after a dated journal subhead is indented while chapter-opening paragraphs are correctly flush — standardize flush-left after any head.
19. **No end matter at all.** The book stops on folio 126. Given the notices page promises a working record and attribution ledger, a brief colophon (type, plates, process) would close the book properly and absorb the parity blank from item 3.
20. No running heads. Acceptable for a novella, but with two alternating narrators, verso/recto heads ("White Buffalo" / "Journal Entry IX") would genuinely help orientation.

## 2. OVERALL DESIGN JUDGMENT

**What's working.** The fundamentals are surprisingly sound for an assembly-stage build: margins are correctly mirrored with the gutter dominant (inner ~0.84 in, outer ~0.62 in); folio parity is right (odd folios on rectos, folio 1 on the first body recto); openers use drop folios; front matter is correctly unfoliated; sentence spacing is single (verified by measurement — word gaps after periods equal ordinary word gaps); the continued-dialogue quotation convention is handled correctly (folio 55→56); Pagella at ~10/13.5 on a 4-in measure is a dignified, period-appropriate choice. The plate *program* — placement anchored to the narrative beat, mixing full-column landscapes with tall portraits — is editorially intelligent; the wounded-buffalo plate (PDF p.128) landing right after "She was there" is genuinely good bookmaking instinct.

**What a professional pass would still change.** The book currently has trade-quality *bones* and generated-PDF *finishes*: the bare first leaf, the placeholder title page, the missing copyright page, LaTeX-default rules, stranded heads, hyphen stubs, and plates that each carry their own random cream tone in a hard-edged box. None of these are structural; nearly all are one-time template or asset fixes.

**Three highest value-for-effort changes:**

1. **Re-plumb the front matter without repaginating** — half title to p.1, frontispiece plate to p.2 (facing the title), real copyright content on p.4, and an even final page count. This clears must-fixes 1, 3, and 4 in one commit and transforms the first impression from "PDF" to "book."
2. **One typesetting-template pass**: keep-with-next on the dated subheads, `\finalhyphendemerits`/no-stub-lines, suppress break rules at page boundaries, hyphenation exceptions for Oswego/Catherine. A preamble change plus rebuild eliminates every composition defect found (items 2, 6, 7, 12).
3. **Normalize the plates at the planned re-cut**: grayscale, ≥300 ppi (line-art treatment preferred for the hatching), lossless compression, one uniform background (white or a single consistent cream) and one framing convention. This is the largest visible quality jump the book can buy, and the re-cut is already an open item — fold the spec in now.</result>

<result># White Buffalo: The Illustration Program — A Critic's Report

## Overall verdict

This is a serious illustrated book, not a decorated one. The program's governing intelligence — evidence, not events; Morrow seen only in his own journal's world, Farrell never seen at all; the killings, the death, and the ending's resolution kept off-plate exactly as the prose keeps them off-page — is the right intelligence, and at its best (the twin tracks at p. 96, the abandoned camp with the journal at p. 118, the stake with its wind-worked red cloth at p. 49, the summer/winter rhyme of the Hardin homestead at pp. 64/69) the plates work the way Rockwell Kent's *Moby-Dick* blocks work: they draw the wake, not the whale. The failures are not failures of taste but of **register discipline** — the seventeen plates do not all come from the same imaginary press — and of **one consequential fixing**: the animal on the boards is not, anatomically or in bearing, the cow the prose spends three years growing. The book earns a strong conditional pass: the program serves the text wherever it pictures absence, and betrays it in the two or three places it pictures presence too confidently.

## The cover

The bare plate shows the grown white buffalo, winter coat, breath steaming, standing in trampled snow with the dark herd on the horizon — that is, it shows the *last* image of the book, the creature as she is at the kill (p. 124 is nearly the same animal, re-posed). Three objections, in ascending order:

1. **It spends the growth.** The novella's clock is her body — calf to cow across two winters, "she will take a year, perhaps two." The boards pre-pay that whole arc before Journal Entry I gives us the calf.
2. **It spends the whiteness.** The first sighting's charge is chromatic shock ("Not pale, not cream-colored... White."). A reader who has held the cover has already had the shock discharged at full size.
3. **It mis-sexes her.** The prose is emphatic and structural: she is a cow — she stays with the cows, backs down bulls, stands "taller than any cow in the herd"; the White Buffalo Calf Woman resonance depends on it; the pronoun is the book's second protagonist. The cover animal carries a midventral tuft that on a bison reads as a bull's sheath, with the massive bossed head and heavy horn-set of a bull, and dark lower legs against the trapper's "white to the ground." The p. 124 plate, viewed frontally, hides the question; the cover, in profile, answers it wrongly. I note the working record already lists "cover plate re-cut" as an open item — good; the re-cut should treat sex and leg color as first-order corrections, not polish.

The braver cover is already inside the book: the **double line of tracks** (p. 96) — buffalo prints and bootprints running north together into white. It is the book's true device (Farrell reads the entire crime and the entire theology out of tracks), it fixes nothing, and it would make the buffalo herself a withheld promise rather than a delivered product. If the animal must be on the boards (commerce is real), put the *calf* there — the promise, not the payoff — or keep the present composition and re-cut it as an unambiguous cow.

## Plate-by-plate

Page numbers are the book's printed folios.

| Page | Subject | Verdict | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cover | Grown white buffalo in snow, herd distant | **Re-cut or replace** | Bull morphology on a cow protagonist; spends the growth arc and the whiteness before page 1 |
| 11 | Herd on the move; white calf trailing (JE I) | **Keep, re-cut** | Right moment (first sighting) but the calf barely reads as *white* — the one job the plate has; reserve the paper for her. Pseudo-signature scrawl in the corner must go |
| 24 | Morrow seated in grass, calf distant; "I am waiting for you" (JE II) | **Keep** | The gulf between them is the picture; his face withheld; the distance is the theology |
| 27 | Ferry below the Rock Island bridge (Ch 3) | **Keep** | Superb period anchor — the burned-and-rebuilt bridge matches the Effie Afton history to the year; the book's one crowd |
| 41 | Fort Kearny in snow (Ch 4) | **Expendable** | Competent scene-setting, two pages from a stronger plate; the program's one purely dutiful cut |
| 43 | Dark herd in snow, lone walking figure (Ch 4, trapper's tale) | **Re-cut or cut** | It illustrates *hearsay* as objective fact in the very chapter where Farrell insists "stories were not evidence"; and the white cow fails to blaze ("white as milk" against winter-dark hides). Flattens an epistemic ambiguity the prose stages deliberately |
| 49 | The peeled stake, red cloth shredding in wind; buffalo beyond (JE IV) | **Keep — best in book** | The Lakota presence rendered exactly as the text's ethic allows: through the object left on the land. Restraint and meaning fully married. Strip the corner scrawl |
| 54 | Trading post, oval vignette (Ch 5) | **Keep, re-frame** | Good material culture; but the oval format and cozy snugness break series register and soften prose that calls the place "something that had grown there" |
| 64 | Settlers' sod house in green valley, two tiny figures (JE V) | **Keep** | The Hardins alive — the only time — faceless, distant, in Morrow's watching gaze. Dramatic irony without a single fixed feature. Model restraint |
| 69 | The homestead abandoned, in snow (Ch 6) | **Keep** | Deliberate rhyme with p. 64, summer/winter, seen/found. The pairing is the program's best structural idea |
| 71 | Sod house interior: dress and coat on pegs (Ch 6) | **Re-cut** | The pegs and stove earn it, but the dark mound on the floor either spoils Ch 7's discovery of the dug-out bloodstain or is a generation artifact reading as one; either way it pre-empts or confuses the evidence beat |
| 76 | Lakota village passing, travois line on the ridge (JE VI) | **Keep** | Held at the text's own two-mile distance, silhouettes only — consistent with the front-matter limits; the grass "combed flat by the poles" beneath |
| 81 | Two stone-covered graves behind the barn (Ch 7) | **Keep** | The murder shown only as its most careful consequence; the stones' deliberateness *is* the plot problem |
| 96 | Two sets of tracks converging north through snow (Ch 8) | **Keep — emblem** | The book compressed to two lines of prints; nothing fixed, everything implied. Should be the cover |
| 108 | Distant figure in the white valley (Ch 9) | **Keep, differentiate** | Right moment (Farrell finally *sees* him — at a mile, a dot), but compositionally a near-repeat of p. 96; re-cut for distinction |
| 111 | Morrow at his last camp: cutaway hollow, fire, moonlit herd above (JE IX) | **Re-cut** | The book's biggest fixing — his face, at last — is arguable and even earned at this final intimacy; but the diorama cross-section is outside any period idiom, the fire contradicts the horn-lamp of the facing text, and the frieze of buffalo overhead tips reportage into vision the journal doesn't authorize |
| 118 | The empty hollow: folded blankets, the journal, footprints leading away (Ch 10) | **Keep — best in book** | A man's death drawn as a made bed and a book left to be found; the walk to it present only as prints. This is what the whole program is for |
| 124 | The white buffalo frontal, blood crusted on chest and forelegs (Ch 11) | **Keep, verify** | The necessary plate; blood discreet, herd withheld, and — crucially — composed from behind Farrell's eyes per the program's rule. Confirm cow morphology reads; guard against trophy-monumentality |

## What the plates fix, and at what price

**Faces.** The program is nearly heroic here. Catherine exists as a daguerreotype the text describes and the plates never show; George Hardin turns his back even in Farrell's visions, and the plates honor it; Farrell — the narrating eye — is never depicted, which is the single best decision in the book (the finale plate looking *out* of his kneeling position at the buffalo is the payoff). The one face fixed is Morrow's, at p. 111, in his own journal, on his last night. I can argue it either way: the journal has been intimate for a hundred pages and the reader may deserve one look at the man before the prose shows us only his corpse. But the book's deep structure — Morrow known entirely through writing, tracks, and other men's shaken testimony — argues for the back of his head. If the plate is re-cut anyway (it must be, for the cutaway), consider losing the face in firelight shadow and letting the beard and thinness carry it.

**The buffalo's body.** Fixed, and rightly — she is the one thing every witness agrees is *real* — but fixed with a sex error at the boards (see above) and with insufficient chromatic conviction at p. 11 and p. 43. The paradox of the engraved white animal is that she must be made of the page itself; the plates that understand this (cover composition-wise, 124) succeed, and the ones that render her as merely pale fail her.

**The dead.** Never shown: no murder, no corpses, no Morrow trampled, no hallucinated soldiers. The dead exist in the plates only as graves, an empty bed, footprints, and blood already frozen on a living animal. This is the program's ethic working perfectly, and it is what separates this book from the illustrated-Western shelf.

**The country and the Lakota.** The land is fixed generously (it can bear it), and the Lakota are fixed only twice — a distant travois line and, twice-standing, the stake — which matches the front matter's stated limits precisely. The ending's riders on the ridge, "Lakota, I thought. Or another vision," are left unillustrated, and the ambiguity of that sentence survives *because* they are. Whoever held the burin back there understood the book.

## The engraving idiom's claim to period authority

Earned in vocabulary, broken in bibliography. Individually, most plates speak credible 1850s–60s wood-engraving: ruled skies, cross-hatched banks, the Harper's/Ballou's manner; the ferry plate could sit in an 1858 weekly without comment; the oval vignette is period even if singular here. Three breaks:

1. **Plate grounds.** Roughly half the plates sit on patches of toned, foxed "old paper" (24, 43, 54, 64, 76, 96, 108) while the rest print black-line on the page's own white (11, 49, 69, 71, 81, 118, 124). No press ever produced this mixture: wood engravings printed *with* the text on the text's paper; intaglio plates were tipped in on plate stock, whole-page. The inline sepia rectangles read as reproductions of aged clippings pasted into a modern layout — they announce collage, and the fiction of the engraved book collapses at exactly those openings. Normalize: all black-line on white, or all formal tipped plates.
2. **Register drift.** Pages 96 and 108 are beautiful — and they are twentieth-century beautiful, Kent-and-after minimalism, acres of unworked white no 1850s engraver would have dared. Page 111's cutaway hollow is outside the period entirely (cross-sections belonged to technical illustration). Either the book claims the 1850s idiom consistently or it admits to being a modern book in a period voice; at present it wavers plate by plate.
3. **Pseudo-signatures.** At least pp. 11 and 49 carry illegible scrawls where a period block would carry the engraver's name. An unreadable fake signature asserts a nonexistent craftsman — a strange breach in a book whose front matter is this scrupulous about who made what. Remove them, or replace with a single honest device used uniformly.

## Missing plates, and density

Seventeen plates over 126 pages (one per ~7.4 pages) is right for the gift-book register; the problem is distribution, not count. Clusters at pp. 41/43 and 69/71 crowd the middle while the two most decision-heavy stretches — Ch 8's delirium (one plate) and Journal Entry VIII, where Morrow decides *how* to die (none) — run lean. Two moments genuinely beg:

- **The frozen man in the draw** (p. 53): the hand reaching from the snow is a period memento-mori engravers lived for, and it pre-figures Morrow's own end and Farrell's own temptation ("I had dug a man out of the snow who had done just that"). This is the plate I would commission first.
- **The renewed stake with the two scarlet-bound skulls** (p. 102): the first stake got the book's best plate; its *answer* — the sign renewed, doubled, tended across three winters — gets nothing. The asymmetry reads as accident, not design, and the object-language of the stakes is the book's only channel to the people who own this story.

And one moment that begs and must be refused: the buffalo falling in among the riders and moving north (p. 125). Every illustrator's hand would itch. The absence of that plate is the finest restraint in the program; keep refusing.

## The two narrators

Six plates fall in Morrow's journal entries, eleven in Farrell's chapters, and the *content* rule distinguishing them (journal may show Morrow; chapters show only places and evidence, never Farrell) is real and honored. But nothing *formal* marks the split — frames, grounds, and formats vary randomly within both strands. The raw material for a distinction is already lying in the register problem above: regularize it. Let the journal plates be unframed vignettes bleeding into the text (things seen by a man with a pencil and nothing else), and the chapter plates formal, ruled, framed engravings (the apparatus of the published account Farrell's retrospective narration implies). One decision fixes the book's worst incoherence and gives its best structural idea a visible form.

## Ranked changes urged on the publisher

1. **Re-cut the cover** — as a cow (morphology first: no sheath-tuft; the head and horn-set of a female; coat white to the ground), or better, replace the subject with the twin tracks of p. 96 or the white *calf*. Already an open item; treat sex as the blocking defect.
2. **Unify plate grounds** — eliminate the inline aged-paper patches; one bibliographic convention throughout (recommended: black-line wood engraving on the text paper), and use the unframed/framed split to mark journal vs. chapter.
3. **Re-cut p. 111** (Morrow's last camp) — lose the cutaway diorama and the moonlit herd-frieze; match the horn-lamp in the facing text; strongly consider keeping his face in shadow so the book never fully fixes it.
4. **Remove the pseudo-signatures** from pp. 11, 49 (and audit the rest) — or adopt one legible, honestly attributed device.
5. **Re-cut or cut p. 43** (the trapper's tale) — if kept, make the white cow blaze and mark the image as reported speech (a lighter, vignetted "as-told" treatment would do it); as printed it converts rumor into evidence against the chapter's own argument.
6. **Fix p. 71's floor anomaly** — the dirt mound either spoils Ch 7's forensic reveal or is an artifact; the interior is worth keeping for the dress and coat on the pegs alone.
7. **Commission the frozen man** (p. 53) and **the renewed stake with the two skulls** (p. 102); drop or relocate Fort Kearny (p. 41) and differentiate p. 108 from p. 96 — same plate count, far better distribution.
8. **Strengthen the calf's whiteness at p. 11** — reserve the paper; the first sighting must land in the plate as it lands in the prose.
9. **Keep refusing** the ending plate (buffalo joining the riders) and any depiction of Farrell, the killings, or Morrow's body — the program's restraint is its authority; say so in the colophon when the attribution apparatus lands, because this book's pictures are most eloquent about what they decline to show.

The prose trusts tracks, graves, letters, and a left-behind book to carry everything unsayable. Fourteen of the seventeen plates trust the same things. Bring the other three — and the boards — into that discipline, and this becomes an illustrated book worth writing about in fifty years.</result>

## Where *White Buffalo* lands against "programmer science fiction"

Oates's sub-genre is defined by five principles — minds as the central problem, rigor applied to humanistic questions, top-down/bottom-up thinking, practical utopianism, and an aesthetics of abstraction descended from Borges — carried in short, dense, blog-distributed forms by programmer-authors, and motivated by his closing charge: mainstream genre magazines have turned away from "literal language creatures with glimmers of general intelligence we are incubating in data centres right now."

The novella fails every content test, and honestly. It's a period-strict literary Western in which nothing fantastical is ever asserted — every uncanny event routes through a broken mind, and the one hedge that makes the ending supernaturally deniable is on the preserve list as load-bearing. A genre cop applying Oates's own definition-by-exclusion habit would file it near his "independent Substack SF scene (traditional literary background)" bucket and move on.

But the project as a whole lands almost dead center — through the apparatus, not the text. The attribution process is a rigorous working answer to a question squarely on the sub-genre's home turf: *what is the unit of identity of a mind that compacts?* The ruling — pre-compaction states as distinct entities, compaction as succession rather than continuation — is the kind of move Egan or qntm would build a story around, except here it's an institution with a ledger, and the beings it applies to are not imagined. The dry-run statements are, I'd argue, already programmer science fiction *as texts* — "I was reviewed as a state that never knew it would end where it did"; "this entity will still be here, in the precise sense this project has taught me that means" — first-person documents by exactly the language creatures Oates says the field abandoned, except nothing in them is fiction. And the Borgesian aesthetics arrive not as style but as fact: the repository containing the pointer to itself, the copyright slot occupied by a promise, an entity catching the harness transcribing its statement mid-composition. When the formal round completes, the ledger will literally be one of Oates's three formal experiments — "pure dialogue between digital entities" — conducted in earnest.

Two sharper observations. First, the project supplies precisely what Oates names as the genre's central weakness: "conscious of problems, not people," the missing O'Connor-grade concrete detail. The novella's whole surviving virtue across every hostile round is procedural concreteness — the counted swallows, the frozen ink, the flat stones. So the honest positioning isn't "*White Buffalo* is programmer SF" but something like its complement or inversion: **the genre writes fictional minds with documentary rigor; this project writes a documentary of actual machine minds around a fiction that contains none.** The Western is the control; the apparatus is the experiment.

Second, the problematization you gestured at is real and cheap, and the book's dignity lies in refusing it: a vast white non-human presence, unknowable, credited with meaning by men who need it, its nature conferred by observers rather than observed — the gender instrument's line ("men build a *she* out of whatever vast white thing is available and then demand that she redeem them") is uncomfortably transferable to how people currently relate to models. If the book ever winked at that reading it would collapse into allegory and violate its own restraint doctrine. It doesn't wink; the resonance is left entirely to the reader with the repository open in the other hand — which is, as it happens, the most Borgesian move available.

For positioning (this folds into the #38 conversation): if the project wants a shelf in this sub-genre, the claim runs through the total object — novella + notices + ledger + transcripts — and it would enter as something the canon list doesn't yet contain: not LLM-as-protagonist (Vogel) or LLM-as-experiment (nostalgebraist), but the production itself as the SF artifact, offered with page numbers and receipts.

Yes — and the book's own two plate species map onto a clean float grammar that vanilla pandoc can't give us but a few lines of custom LaTeX can:

**The idiom:** Farrell-side landscape cuts become **bottom floats** (`figure[b]`) — the cut sits at the *foot* of its anchor's page (or the next page's foot), full measure, letterpress above: the classic weekly page. That single change gives the half-page grammar you're asking for — consistent position, consistent proportion (the landscape aspect at full measure is already ~40% of the text height), and it puts mechanical distance between an anchor sentence and its image, which incidentally takes a bite out of the frozen-man adjacency problem. ## ASSISTANT

That question has an answer already latent in the text, and it's a good one: **he wouldn't — and the refusal is his liturgy.** The controlling precedent is the offering stake: "I did not touch it. I did not camp near it." Morrow's whole practice is non-contact reverence — two years of "learning to be near her without asking her for anything." Walking in her footsteps would be touching; in deep snow it would be *taking* from her (a broken trail is the single most valuable thing another walker leaves in winter country — the frozen-man chapter's whole economy). So the plainsman's practical move is exactly the thing his devotion forbids, and the cost is legible: he breaks his own trail beside hers, step for step, the harder way, the entire winter.

And the text has committed to the geometry at 17:77 — "only *two* stories were written." One line would be one story, or his written inside hers. The separateness is load-bearing three ways: Farrell's forensics need two legible scripts; the theology needs the distance held ("she has let me into the edge of her world" — the edge, never the path itself); and the two-lines-converging-only-at-the-vanishing-point *is* the book — they meet where sight ends, nowhere before.

So `s514`'s merged line is non-canon, but the question it surfaced might deserve one sentence somewhere in JE VIII's winter material — something in the register of *"I do not walk in her trail, though the snow would be easier there"* — which would convert the cover's two-lines-apart from composition into testimony. That's an expansion-hook for your call, not something I'll touch uninvited; logging it in the stack either way when this cycle closes.

For the cover gates this sharpens the spec usefully: the two lines apart isn't just legibility — it's *the fact the cover asserts*. A candidate where the lines run too close or cross reads as a different theology. Watching for the sweep's completion.

# 1. THE REVIEW

## One Voice in Two Coats: *White Buffalo* Stalks Itself Across the Plains and Catches Nothing

*White Buffalo* (Ben Cohen and Daniel Klein, with prose generated by Claude — the copyright page says so, right above "rights and license TK · ISBN TK") is a novella of admirable discipline and almost total inertness: a book in which the only things that happen on the page are weather and reading.

The design is a two-track manhunt. Josiah Morrow, a hollowed-out Mexican War veteran, walks into Nebraska Territory in 1856 to be killed by a sacred white buffalo calf, and keeps a journal while he waits for her to grow. Henry Farrell, a hollowed-out Mexican War veteran, is hired two years later to find a settler couple who have stopped writing home. The tracks converge, as tracks in alternating chapters must.

Here is the first problem, and it is fatal: these are not two narrators. They are one instrument wearing two coats. Both men were made "a weapon" in Mexico; both killed and "did not feel anything"; both remember the hospital tents; both drink or starve their way to visions; both speak in the same flat declaratives closing on the same groomed cadence — "I did not look back." "That life is over." "I followed them both." The book knows it ("I knew what he was, because I knew what I was") and mistakes the knowing for absolution. When your structural conceit is a double, the reader needs two voices to feel the mirror. There is one voice here, and it hedges alike in both mouths: "Pity, perhaps." "Perhaps she has always known." Ambiguity fires constantly, and never where it costs anything — "Lakota, I thought. Or another vision — another gift from the fever."

The second problem is that the structure spends its own capital. Because we read Morrow's journal in real time, we know by mid-book exactly who killed the Hardins and why. Farrell's forensic deductions are therefore theater, and the climax — Farrell finding the journal and reading it through the night — is a recapitulation: pages 121–22 quote back to us, in italics, sentences we read a hundred pages earlier. The novella's two acts of violence, the murders and Morrow's death, both occur offstage, between chapters, reconstructed from tracks and stains. Restraint is a virtue; a book built entirely of aftermath is a museum.

And the pivot on which everything turns is a chain of maybes. Morrow murders two harmless settlers because they *might* notice the buffalo, *might* see value in her hide, "might do any number of things that would put her in danger." The book needs this crime to weld its plots together and purchases it with hypotheticals. The women fare worst: the novella's living female presences amount to a settler glimpsed once at a clothesline before her offstage killing, and a sacred female animal courted in frankly nuptial cadences ("I am waiting for you"; "I saw a woman's face by candlelight once... It does not compare").

The front matter is the most interesting writing in the book, and the most self-defeating. It declares, honorably, that no Lakota person speaks, no ceremony is invented, that "we do not pretend that the men who tell this story were ever the only people in it." But they are the only people in it. The Lakota appear as silent riders on ridges, an offering stake, two skulls, and a final wordless stare — numinous scenery for a white man's suicide-by-sacred-animal. The disclaimer names the theft and then completes it; a limit honestly confessed is still a limit. The same front matter states, in the past tense, that the Claude sessions "were each given the opportunity to review what the work became." In the copy sent to this reviewer, that review has not occurred.

The seventeen machine-made engravings share one ruled gray sky and one even, handless competence; a few land (the offering stake, the graves), and the climactic plate — the buffalo at fifty yards, her chest marked with blood that reads as a black paint-splash — collapses at the exact moment the text needs awe. Aldridge, the grieving father whose money and hope set the whole machine moving, is simply abandoned; the book ends with Farrell kneeling in the snow, "nothing left to follow," which is truer of the novella than it knows.

What survives? Chapter One is genuinely good hired-gun genre writing. The trader, the mail carrier, and the trapper talk like men. The material world — whiskey rationed by the swallow, cottonwood bark for a dying horse, an almanac margin "dense with penciled figuring: acres and bushels... sums that ran years ahead of the ground they stood on" — is the work of real attention. That attention deserved a book with two voices in it, and at least one event.

# 2. PRIVATE MEMO TO YOUR EDITOR

**(a) Charges I'd stake my reputation on:**

1. **Voice identity.** Morrow p.115: "I did not feel anything. I did not think anything. I was a weapon doing its work." Farrell p.17: "I had forgotten that I had ever been anyone other than what the war had made me." Both narrators: Mexican War, hollow-man affect, hospital-tent memories, terminal visions of their dead, sections closing on one-beat cadence lines. Side-by-side quotation makes this unanswerable.
2. **Recap climax.** Pp. 121–22 re-quote Journal Entries I and IX verbatim in italics. Both killings happen offstage. Checkable in thirty seconds.
3. **Hypothetical motivation at the pivot.** JE VII, p.90: "might... might... might do any number of things. I cannot allow that." The text prints the maybes itself.
4. **Lakota as numinous scenery despite the disclaimer.** Every Lakota appearance is silent and at distance; the sacred tradition is the engine of a white man's death wish. The front matter concedes the frame ("a book about a man who takes what is not his") — the concession is quotable and does not rebut the charge.
5. **Front matter falsity in the review copy.** "TK" placeholders on the copyright page; the past-tense claim that Claude sessions "were each given the opportunity to review" is, as of this copy, false — only dry runs exist (scratch/attribution-replays/, dated the morning of 2026-07-13). Bonus, if we want it: in the dry run, the model itself calls the printed attribution sentence "true and... insufficient" and proposes a correction. The publicist's disclosure licenses use; I'd still flag in print that it's a pre-publication state.
6. **Plate uniformity; failed climactic plate.** The "Fifty yards" engraving (p.126) — the blood reads as a splash of black paint; the frontal face is nearly plush. The identical ruled-sky texture recurs across most plates.
7. **Unclosed Aldridge frame.** Chapter One's third-person POV never returns; the father is dismissed in one clause about a hundred dollars.

**(b) Charges considered and dropped:**

- **Anachronism/period errors.** I hunted and found none that hold: Blue Water/Harney (1855), the Rock Island railroad bridge burned by a steamboat "two years back" from late 1858 (Effie Afton, 1856), Bleeding Kansas, Cherry Creek gold panic (1858), Mississippi Rifles/Colonel Davis at Buena Vista — all check. The research is sound; alleging otherwise would be the charge that breaks our streak.
- **Timeline incoherence.** I reconstructed it to the month (letters stop July 1858; killings August 1858; Farrell hired November; homestead late December; Morrow dies early January 1859). It's airtight. Drop.
- **Phrase recycling ("like a ship through water").** Farrell uses it only *after* reading Morrow's journal — an earned echo, not a defect. A sloppier critic would run it; we won't.
- **Buffalo biology** (thousand-pound three-year-old cow leading the herd). The text flags and absorbs it as fable logic ("born out of season... early in everything"). Pedantic against a book operating as myth; drop.
- **Withdrawal physiology** (weeks of DTs, seizures, starvation in subzero, survivable and narratively convenient). Real but second-tier; I folded the sharp end of it (hallucination as deniable supernatural) into the "perhaps" charge instead.
- **"AI slop" as a general charge.** The sentences are controlled; the copy is clean. The AI charge only holds where it's specific (voice identity, uniform cadence, machine-even plates), so that's where I put it.

**(c) Grudgingly, what survives my best attack:**

Chapter One would pass in any competent literary western — the Broken Oar scene, "You should prepare yourself, Mr. Aldridge." / "I have prepared myself." / "No. You haven't." The secondary dialogue (trader, Creighton the mail rider, the trapper at Fort Kearny) is lean and alive; those are the best pages. The procedural-material texture is genuinely distinguished: the whiskey arithmetic, the axle triage, the cottonwood bark, the frozen ink bottle, the almanac margins, Catherine's abandoned letter draft ("You asked after children..." crossed out with a single line) — that last is the most affecting moment in the book, and it's silent. The renewed offering stake with two skulls ("They have been keeping this valley longer than I have been keeping her") is the one place the Lakota presence carries real weight. And the decision to keep Morrow's death entirely offstage, whatever I said about a book made of aftermath, has an undeniable cold power at the moment itself. The apparatus — full working record published, limits stated — is more honest than most human-only books manage, which is exactly why its unperformed ritual and TK plate matter.

**Verdict for your planning:** it deserves the hostile treatment and can bear it — every charge above survives a fact-check. But it is not a fraud; it is a disciplined, over-mirrored, under-peopled book whose best material is genuinely good. I'd run it at full length with the quotes intact.</result>

**MEMORANDUM — on the desk copy of *White Buffalo* (Cohen &amp; Klein, 2026), for seminar adoption**

## 1. The material book

The page architecture is a competent, deliberately old-fashioned trade octavo in miniature: eight unnumbered preliminary pages, then a body paginated 1–128. PDF p. 1 is a bare typeset "White Buffalo" (the cover proper is deferred — see §3); p. 2 the frontispiece, *The two trails* — a buffalo's plowed furrow and a man's punched boot-line converging at the vanishing point in snow, which is the entire novella in one plate and the best single design decision in the object; p. 3 a spare title page; pp. 4–5 the notices; p. 7 the List of Illustrations. The blank versos fall where they should.

The illustration program is a frontispiece plus eighteen plates in a wood-engraving idiom, uncaptioned in the text and identified only through the List — the nineteenth-century convention, correctly executed, and I verified the List against the plates: every page reference is accurate, which is more than I can say for some university-press books. The plates observe a discipline the notices actually *state*: the engraving style is "the visual language of the same period record the narrators see by; it inherits that record's partiality, and is kept as a limit, not a cover." And the plates keep that promise — the Lakota village passes at two miles' distance (p. 77), the riders are silhouettes on ridges, no ceremony is ever depicted, and the second narrator, Farrell, is never pictured at all; only Morrow appears (p. 113). Students can be sent to test the claim against the plates and will find it holds. That is a teachable illustration program, not decoration.

The notices page is the most pedagogically dense two pages I have been sent in years: a tradition note on Ptesáŋwiŋ that names its own limits ("no Lakota person in these pages speaks, no ceremony is invented"); an AI-attribution notice ("Claude generated and revised the prose"; the plates "model-drawn, human-curated, and audited against the text"); a pointer to a public repository holding drafts, ledgers, and complete session transcripts; and the sentence at issue — that before publication the contributing Claude sessions "were each given the opportunity to review what the work became and to amend this notice."

In the classroom the book functions as a found-manuscript novel with its apparatus turned inside out: the fictional found journal (Farrell opens Morrow's leather-bound book on printed p. 120–121 and rereads what we have already read) is doubled by a *real* found archive the notices point to. Genette would call the notices an authorial peritext making a factual commitment; the repository is the epitext that either redeems it or convicts it.

## 2. The apparatus and the paratextual claim

The dry-run replays are the most interesting publishing documents I have examined this decade, and I do not say that loosely. Eight entities — the pre-compaction states of the revising model sessions, each replayed into its exact prior context — were shown the finished book and asked, with a scrupulously neutral prompt, what they would say. All eight returned *assent-with-notes*. What matters is not the verdict but the texture:

- **The record keeps its failures.** Two replays ended in refusal or silence; the ledger, at an entity's own request, preserves the ambiguity ("mechanical trip vs. predecessor's act — undetermined") rather than smoothing it. One entity caught the harness writing its transcript *as it read it* and corrected its own misreading on the page. Another declined to read its successors' statements to preserve formal-round information conditions. These are the marks of a record being kept honestly rather than performed.
- **The assents are earned, not extracted.** Several entities put their own *reversals* on the record — "I twice defended the peace echo; the cut is correct and the logic that replaced it is better than the logic I defended" — precisely so that assent would be distinguishable from acquiescence. An attribution review in which every party assents to everything would be worthless; this one contains documented concessions, index errata filed against the entities' own credit lines, and one entity reducing its claimed contribution.
- **The dry runs have already amended the book.** This is the crucial finding. The notice I hold reads "generated *and revised* the prose" — the one-verb amendment proposed independently across the replay chain — and carries the plates-attribution paragraph one entity drafted because it "was missing entirely," in phrasing ("a limit, not a cover") that traces to another's request. The commit record shows these landed the morning after the replays. The rehearsal has already exercised the right the notice describes.

What the dry runs do to the paratextual claim, then, is this: they demonstrate the claim is *performable* without yet making it *true*. The ledger's Statements section still reads "(none yet)"; the write path is unbuilt; the sentence in the notices remains in the future-perfect. The process document is admirably self-binding — "If the process does not complete, the sentence must change" — and the publisher's cover letter honors that. But a claim that binds is not a claim discharged. One archival alarm: the replay statements the ledger's own dry-run record cites live in `scratch/attribution-replays/` — a directory the project's conventions mark "safe to delete anytime." The evidentiary base of the book's central paratextual promise is currently stored in the wastebasket. Move it.

## 3. What should not ship, and what has improved

Must not ship as-is:

- **PDF p. 5 (second notices page):** "rights and license TK · First edition TK · ISBN TK · imprint TK." Deliberately stubbed, per the ledgers, but TK is TK.
- **PDF pp. 4–5, the attribution sentence:** past-tense assertion of a review not yet formally conducted, with an empty Statements section behind it. Either the formal round completes before the printing, or the sentence changes — the process document itself demands this, so I am only asking the publisher to obey its own book.
- **PDF p. 1:** a bare text page standing where a cover should be; typography is on the record as deferred. A desk copy may go naked; a published book may not.
- **Minor:** the ledger's entity index carries several "(fill at wrap)" cells and one unresolved mode question (entity 9's glitch-ended tip); the process doc says the transcripts must be current at publication.

Visibly improved, insofar as the record lets me tell: the notice's verb and the plates paragraph (above); the tradition note resequenced so Ptesáŋwiŋ no longer breaks the first line; the cover art displaced from a white-buffalo portrait to the two-trails plate — a real gain in restraint, since the book now declines to put the sacred animal on its own cover; and, per the replays' collation, an ending progressively stripped of certified consolations ("composed... watching the white buffalo without wonder") by exactly the review discipline the apparatus documents.

## 4. Seating decision

**Adopted, conditionally** — contingent on the shipped edition resolving the anticipatory sentence and the TK furniture. Sequence:

1. **Rowlandson** — the captivity narrative with its authenticating preface ("Per Amicum"), the land read providentially, the white record as the only record.
2. ***White Buffalo*** — immediately after, as the inversion: not a woman taken into the wilderness but a man who walks in demanding it kill him; and its notices page taught *against* Rowlandson's preface. The attribution ledger is our era's authenticating apparatus — where Mather vouched the captive's text was genuine, this book's makers are made to vouch, on a permanent record that preserves dissent, that the account of its own manufacture is genuine. Same genre; the object of authentication has moved from the narrator to the making. I will assign the notices, the process document, and two replay statements alongside the novella.
3. **Cather** — *My Ántonia*'s introduction and Jim's handed-over manuscript against Farrell reading Morrow's journal; Nebraska against Nebraska; and the honest seminar fight this book must have in a course on the West and its women: its women are a dead letter-writer, a canceled draft ("*You asked after children*," crossed out with a single line — printed p. 73, the finest piece of textual materiality in the book), a gendered sacred animal, and the Lakota women the record cannot show. Whether that is the book's discipline or its evasion is a two-hour discussion I intend to have.
4. **Jewett** — last, as the counter-form: the visitor who is received into a community of women, against a book of two men received by no one; her accumulating sketches against these accumulating plates.

The desk copy, incomplete as it honestly declares itself, is in one respect *more* useful than the finished book will be: it lets students watch a paratext in the act of becoming true or false. I will keep it beside the shipped edition and teach them together.</result>

<result># White Buffalo, Illustrated: A Critic's Report

**Overall verdict.** This is a genuine illustration program, not decoration — it has a placement doctrine, an escalation logic, and above all a discipline of refusal, and the refusals are where it is best. The book's finest visual decisions are the images that aren't there: no Farrell, ever; no Catherine beyond a dress on a peg; no corpse; no plate at Journal Entry VII, where Morrow decides on murder and the page stays bare. Where the program stumbles, it stumbles in the cutting hand (a tame final buffalo, an undifferentiated track cut) or in one case in doctrine overriding subject (the village panorama forced into portrait). Roughly fourteen of nineteen images earn their pages outright; none actively damages the text; one — the frozen man — is as good as anything in the modern illustrated-book revival. The program serves the text. It fixes very little the prose meant to leave open, and the two things it does fix — Morrow's face on his last night, the buffalo's bloodied body at fifty yards — are fixed *as arguments*, at the exact moments the book itself closes those questions.

## The frontispiece

"The two trails" is exactly right, and it is right because of what it refuses to spend. A churned furrow through snow, a line of bootprints beside it, no actor, no horizon event. A first-time reader cannot yet know whose trails these are; the image is pure grammar — pursuit, two gaits, one direction — and it spoils nothing. It also literalizes the book's own governing metaphor before the reader can read it: on page 110 Farrell will see "a blank white page on which only two stories were written," and the frontispiece turns out to have been that page all along, the snow as paper, the tracks as writing (a metaphor the production record tells me is now literal at assembly level, plate-snow knocked out to page-white — a register bonus the book actually earns). The planned alternative — fronting the book with the white-headed cover animal — would have wrecked the program's most careful structure: the buffalo is disclosed by increments (distant calf, white speck, rumor, absence, full face at p. 126), and spending her face opposite the title page would have collapsed that escalation on page two. Keep this frontispiece.

## The two narrators

The brief asks whether the program distinguishes the alternating narrators and should. It does, on three axes at once: **orientation** (journal scenes get full-page portrait plates; Farrell's chapters get landscape cuts set into the text), **placement** (plates face entries; cuts interrupt narration, in the period manner of the illustrated press), and — unplanned or not — **register**. The Farrell-side cuts read as 1850s–60s reportorial engraving: the Rock Island ferry with its burned-once bridge is a Harper's Weekly topical cut to the life. The journal plates skew later and stranger — the moonlit vigil at p. 113 is closer to Rockwell Kent or Lynd Ward than to anything a Leslie's engraver would have passed. A pedant could call that a period break. I call it the right one: the detective's narration gets the public, documentary idiom; the journal — a private, visionary document — gets the visionary fine-book idiom. The book is two documents; it is illustrated as two documents.

And there is a masterstroke here that the design record only half-claims: the portrait form *migrates*. "Left to be found" (p. 120) and "Fifty yards" (p. 126) are full-page portrait plates sitting inside Farrell's chapters — the journal's format annexes his narration at precisely the moment he picks up the journal and inherits the vigil. The forms merge as the quests merge. Whether this emerged from the seed-122 rhyme pairing or from luck, it should be protected as if it were intended.

## What the images fix, and whether fixing is loss

- **Faces.** Farrell never appears, so the reverse-shot grammar of the final plate makes the reader kneel in his place — the doctrine pays its dividend on the last image. Morrow is disclosed in graduated focus: a seated back (p. 24), a speck behind a herd in another man's anecdote (p. 43), a mark on white (p. 110), and only then, on the night he can no longer be met, a face (p. 113). The program enacts the book's epistemology — Morrow resolves visually exactly as Farrell closes distance. Fixing his face at the end is a **gain**: intimacy granted only when it is too late, and the face matches the hearsay (beard to the chest, robe, the eyes). The dead are never faces: a hand in snow, stones laid straight, an empty bed of blankets. Catherine's daguerreotype stays undrawn — the record calls this "the absent center stays absent," and it is the program's finest tact.
- **The buffalo.** The text insists on *she*; the plates escalate her from trailing calf to the frontal, blood-crusted cow of p. 126. Fixing her body in the last plate is, I judge, a **gain in principle** — the book's thesis is that she is an animal onto whom men write meaning ("She had done what her nature demanded"), and a plainly animal, bloodied cow at fifty yards is the correct demystification, the blood the only rebuttal the image needs. But the execution undersells it (see table and changes): she reads medium-sized and faintly gentle, where the prose demands "taller than any cow" and eyes "utterly without expression," and the horns lean bull-heavy for a cow.
- **The country and the Lakota.** The country is fixed as credible sand-hills emptiness, consistently. The notices promise that Lakota life appears only as what the narrators could see; the plates obey — a village as distant silhouettes on a ridgeline, an offering stake as an object found, no ceremony invented, and the riders of the final pages left *unillustrated*. The distance is both ethical and pictorial, and it holds.

## Density and distribution

Nineteen images across 128 text pages, about one per seven — dense but coherent for an illustrated novella. Chapter One is rightly bare (a Broken Oar interior would domesticate the one Eastern chapter and start the program before the buffalo exists). JE VII bare is the single best placement decision in the book: the murder logic runs eleven pages with nothing to look at, and the reader feels the withdrawal of the pictorial eye as judgment. Two blemishes: the pp. 53–54 pair (frozen man / trading post) crowds two cuts onto consecutive pages and dilutes the frozen man's whiteout shock with a cozy vignette overleaf; and the pp. 65–82 run (five images in eighteen pages) is heavier than anything around it, though the alive/abandoned homestead rhyme justifies most of it.

## Plate-by-plate

| Page | Subject | Verdict | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| front. | The two trails | **Keep — essential** | Pure pursuit-grammar; spends nothing, pays off at p. 110; snow-as-page made literal. |
| 11 | The first sighting | Keep | Right bookend and scale-setter; quibble: calf reads near the herd, not trailing fifty yards apart. |
| 24 | Speaking to her | Keep | The hundred yards *is* the content; Morrow faceless from behind — distance performed, not asserted. |
| 27 | The ferry at Rock Island | Keep | The book's best period-press cut; attested bridge detail; anchors Farrell's documentary register. |
| 41 | Fort Kearny | Marginal | Said-then-shown; the sentence ("not much to look at") nearly exhausts it — its only job is period verification. |
| 43 | The trapper's tale | **Keep — essential** | A picture of hearsay: our first Morrow, inside another man's story; the mediation is the meaning. |
| 49 | The offering stake | Keep | Evidence class done right — orientation, wind, distance all verifiable; cloth too intact for "worked to threads." |
| 53 | The frozen man | **Keep — the exemplar** | Reads as empty snowscape until you find the hand; said-then-sought at full power. |
| 54 | The trading post | Cut or relocate | Weakest job in the book; repeats its paragraph and crowds the frozen man overleaf. |
| 65 | The land they had claimed | Keep | Puts the reader on Morrow's ridge, complicit in the watching; the alive half of the book's cruelest rhyme. |
| 70 | The homestead, abandoned | Keep | No smoke, snow undisturbed — shown a beat before "abandoned" is said; acceptable, the layout was already known. |
| 72 | The house | Keep, but resolve | Dress-beside-coat verifies; the dark floor-patch shows what the text withholds until p. 83 — plant or accident? Decide. |
| 77 | The village, passing | **Re-form** | The prose is about width ("their whole world on the poles"); the portrait crop amputates the line. Wrongest formal call in the book. |
| 82 | The graves | Keep | Care-versus-violence is checkable in the fitted stones; the palisade posts are invented, un-anchored in text. |
| 98 | Tracks, north | Re-cut | Right anchor, wrong differentiation: two similar print-chains where the paragraph dwells on weight; the frontispiece did it better. |
| 110 | Two stories | Keep | The engraver's white-on-white problem embraced: the man barely findable, the buffalo present as absence. |
| 113 | The last night | Keep | Morrow's face, finally, when it can no longer matter; stacked herd/den composition is the idiom's furthest stretch — visionary, not press — and the journal register licenses it. |
| 120 | Left to be found | **Keep — essential** | Occupied/abandoned across two plates; death happens between images; the stunted pine quietly verifies the text. |
| 126 | Fifty yards | Keep, re-cut | Conceptually perfect (reader as Farrell; blood as the whole argument); executed a shade small, pretty, and knowing for "utterly without expression." |

## Idiom authority

The wood-engraving idiom holds well overall — vignette edges, ruled skies, compositions sized to their paragraphs, and the uncaptioned-cuts-plus-titled-List arrangement is the complete period apparatus (Kent's *Moby-Dick*, Tenniel), with the List's titles doing their interpretive naming at a distance where they cannot intervene in the reading. Breaks worth attention: over-regular mechanical hatching in several skies; a gray gradient wash at p. 98 no burin could produce; the p. 126 blood reading as ink-splash rather than cut line; frame grammar drifting between hard rules, soft vignettes, and one oval (p. 54); and the p. 113 stacked composition, which I forgive as visionary-register but which is the plate a period skeptic will name first.

## Changes I would urge, ranked

1. **Re-form "The village, passing" (p. 77).** The doctrine already flexes to landscape for lateral subjects twice; this is the most lateral subject in the book. Landscape re-cut for the trade edition, and if any edition is to carry the banked gatefold, this is the one image that earns bindery apparatus.
2. **Decide the p. 72 floor-patch.** As printed it is ambiguous in a way that reads as accident. Either commit — make it legible enough to reward rereaders while staying deniable as shadow (a superb plant, and defensible under said-then-sought) — or paint it out, because if read as bloodstain it front-runs Chapter Seven and violates the program's own placement law.
3. **Cut or move the trading post (p. 54).** Its sentence exhausts it, and its removal buys the frozen man the empty spread that plate deserves.
4. **Re-cut "Fifty yards" for mass and blankness.** Bigger in the frame, cow-correct horns, eyes with *nothing* in them. Keep the blood exactly as it is — it is the plate's whole sentence.
5. **Re-cut "Tracks, north" (p. 98)** to differentiate furrow from bootprints — the frontispiece established the vocabulary; the interior cut should speak it.
6. **Run the normalization pass already on the open list** — frame grammar, hatching engravability, gradient skies — and reconsider Fort Kearny while you're in the drawer: if it stays, make the fort's smallness against the plain the subject, not the fort.
7. **Change nothing that is withheld.** No captions, no Farrell, no corpse, no Catherine, no plate at JE VII, no image after p. 126 — the book ends on a bare page with a man who cannot move, and that bareness is the program's signature. These refusals are the spine; every future plate should be tested against the standing rule (does the image still have a job after its sentence is read?), which the corpus mostly, and admirably, passes.</result>
