General finding first: the journal strand's slack is not evenly distributed. Entries I–VI carry nearly all of it — the watcher/waiter/she-grows loop is stated in full roughly nine times before the settlers appear, and almost every entry closes on a groomed cadence line or a promise of arrival ("she will be ready," "that moment is coming," "I can wait"). Entries VII–IX tighten dramatically because they finally have material. The tracker's chapters are tighter throughout; their slack is mostly duplication (mission restated three times, turn-back deliberated three times, the cabin-winter withdrawal story told four times).

---

TEXT: "A year and a half. / It was spring of eighteen fifty-six when I first saw her ... She has changed in that time. So have I."
DIAGNOSIS: Pure recap. Every fact — first sighting (JE I), the purpose, the winter (JE IV) — is owned by the reader; "She has changed. So have I" is the loop's null statement. The date header alone does the calendar work, and the Sept 15 entry does the she-has-changed work in specifics.
LOSES: A soft on-ramp into the entry cluster after a chapter break. Nothing else.

**2. [T1]** — 16-journal-entry-viii.md, *January the Fourth* — final two paragraphs.

DIAGNOSIS: Verbatim pre-spend of JE IX's climax: JE IX ends "This is the right thing. The only right thing I have ever done" and opens its own "To whoever finds this journal" address. Two terminal addresses one entry apart, sharing the book's key phrase, dull the second one. End the entry at "then this is the end of my account."
LOSES: Nothing. JE IX does both gestures better, and gains force by doing them once.

**3. [T1]** — 05-chapter-three.md, tavern-night section, before Council Bluffs.

DIAGNOSIS: Near-verbatim duplicate of Chapter Two's closer ("Somewhere in that emptiness, George and Catherine Hardin had built their homestead, and I would find out what had happened to them"), plus a danger catalog already owned via Hennessey and the tavern talk. Third statement of the mission in two chapters.
LOSES: Nothing but the echo.

DIAGNOSIS: Third beauty declaration (JE III Oct 23, JE V May 18), fourth-plus sacred declaration, and the ready/wait loop at its most naked — every sentence except one is restatement. The one new thing is biographical grain.

Checkpoint committed (36c026a) — the five reversals are in, the book rebuilt clean (30,797 words, down from ~32.1k; plates re-flowed to new folios), and nothing else gets touched until you rule. On the italics: I'd keep them, and I think the manuscript turns out to be consistent under the right rule. Chapter Seven and Ten frame their imagined addresses as *speech* ("I would say," "I could tell him") and set them roman; Chapter Eight frames it as a *document* ("I could return to Aldridge with my report—") and sets it italic — which matches the book's italics-for-written-matter convention exactly (Catherine's letters, the journal quotations). Roman = imagined speech, italic = document content. Q4 resolves as no-change with a principled rule, unless you'd rather flatten it.

The discussion items, one at a time:

**1. Farrell's early dangerousness (Ch 2 enumeration).** The current stitch — "What I would do when I found the truth was not complicated. These things rarely were." — is hard-boiled, but you're right that it's elliptical where the original was plain: *"If she was dead and her husband had killed her, I would kill him."* That's the earliest moment Farrell says the word in his own voice, and with it cut, his first plain "kill" doesn't arrive until Chapter Seven. That's a flinch by relocation even if no single sentence flinches. **My recommendation: restore the full enumeration.** The flat bookkeeping list is the unflinching version *and* the characterization; the Ch 3 duplicate (which contained no kill talk) stays cut, so the mission is now stated once by Aldridge in negotiation and once by Farrell in cold arithmetic — the right two.

**2. JE VI Nov 19 ("what she was made to do").** You're right, and it's worse than load-bearing — it's the setup for a designed collapse. Nov 19's naive theory ("she will turn on me. The instinct that has kept her wary will become the instinct that drives her to attack") is exactly what JE VIII Sept 28 dismantles: "I have assumed that when the time came, the way would be clear. It is not clear... she will not charge." Without the Nov 19 assumption on the page, VIII's correction references nothing, and the manufactured-death arc (through "Or I will have chosen it for her") loses its first rung. **Proposed shape:** keep the scene opening + candlelight comparison, then restore: "And she will kill me. Someday—next autumn, perhaps, or the autumn after—she will turn on me. The instinct that has kept her wary will become the instinct that drives her to attack. And when that happens, I will not run. I will not fight. I will stand before her and let her do what she was made to do." End there — the "She is sacred / I am ready / so I wait" scaffolding stays cut, the naive theory returns whole.

**3. JE VI Dec 1 ("I do not dream anymore").** Agree on both halves: the settlers-dreaming-of-children paragraph is cheap pathos (and pre-empted by Farrell's own discovery of the crossed-out draft one chapter earlier — the reader has *held* that answer; Morrow imagining it generically is a downgrade). But the no-dream declaration is true, cheap in the good sense, and buys the Farrell contrast — his dreams are the book's fulcrum, so Morrow's "I do not dream anymore" is a twin-axis data point. **Proposed shape:** entry ends "...the vigil I have kept and will keep for however long it takes. / I do not dream anymore. I do not think of the future beyond the moment when she and I will face each other for the last time." The weather-coming simile stays cut (a promise closer before a winter the book skips) — say the word if you want it back.

**4. "They are not part of the world I inhabit now."** We are *not* clear to remove — my earlier flag undersold it. The editor read it as a duplicate of JE V's "They were simply there, like the grass and the sky," but the two lines point opposite directions: JE V says the settlers don't register (they're landscape); Nov 5 says *he* is the one outside the world — the exclusion has migrated from them to him, watching the steam-cup domesticity. It rhymes with July 2's "the commandments were written for living men, and I have not been one for two years" and pre-echoes Farrell's "back to the living world" in the final chapter. **Recommendation: restore.** (The "little house, little life" cut in the same entry stands — that dedup against JE VII, where the sneer curdles into the decision, is clean.)

**5. JE VIII terminal address — the dress rehearsal.** The honest case both ways. For the cut: the book's climactic sentence occurs twice ten pages apart, and second occurrences are always cheaper; ending VIII on "If not, then this is the end of my account" sets up JE IX's opening ("This is the end of my account") as an echo fulfilled. For the restore — your side, and I think the stronger one: the duplication *is* the hamartiology. Morrow drafts his testament the night before and performs it again at the end — the self-narrativizing man rehearsing his best line is exactly the curation behavior the book convicts him of everywhere else, and "willingly, gladly" is real matter (it's what the club's yes-camp built its case on). **Middle path, my actual recommendation:** restore the address but let the rehearsal be imperfect — keep "...I am going to my death willingly, gladly." and drop only "with the certainty that it is the only right thing I have ever done," plus restore "The white buffalo is waiting for me. I will not make her wait much longer." The rehearsal does its work; the exact climax phrase fires once, in JE IX, where it must.

Rule on these five and I'll apply precisely what you choose. After that, the untouched holds remain for the same one-at-a-time treatment: the JE VI Sept 8 recap entry, JE IX's three items (thesis restatement, "I am going to die today," the broken-mind concession), JE VIII's "great and quiet peace," JE I's three deep cuts (waiting stack, "By her.", balance-or-joke — that last I'd flatly decline), and Ch 7's ghosts passage, which is entangled with your open shell/ghost ruling.

> A year and a half.

> It was spring of eighteen fifty-six when I first saw her, white against the brown grass, moving apart from the herd—when I understood what I must do, and what I must wait for. Since then, two summers of walking and watching, and one winter that tried its best to kill me.

The editor's case: pure recap — first sighting owned since JE I, the purpose owned since JE I, the winter owned since JE IV; the date header alone does the calendar work; and "She has changed in that time. So have I" is the null statement of the loop, with Sept 15 doing the she-has-changed work in specifics one entry later.

The defense: this is the stagger's consolidation point. JE VI opens right after Farrell finds the graves in December 1858, and the reader vaults back to September 1857 — the widest whiplash in the book. The reading-club instruments identified the JE V "double-click" as the book's strongest structural effect, but the club's nurse also told us she rode the first half believing the strands were simultaneous. This entry is the one place Morrow does the arithmetic out loud, and it arrives exactly where a recovering-from-the-click reader needs it confirmed.

**My recommendation — compress, don't delete:**

> A year and a half. Two summers of walking and watching, and one winter that tried its best to kill me.

One paragraph, ledger-flat, which is his voice at its best. It keeps the calendar consolidation and the entry's function as an on-ramp; it cuts the thesis recap ("when I understood what I must do, and what I must wait for" — the reader has owned this for sixty pages) and the null closer. The entry stops promising and just counts.

Your call: compress as above, delete outright, or keep as-is.

Resolution math first: the in-text landscape plates print at ~4.6in wide, so 2432px ≈ **530 DPI** — past the 300 DPI tone-image standard and into line-art territory; the portrait plates land ~520 DPI and a 2×'d gatefold ~360 DPI over its 10.1in spread. Another doubling would exceed what any press resolves for grayscale work while doubling drift risk per refinement pass. **We're at target — no further bump.** That greenlights the grayscale work, where the added resolution is exactly what lets us push mids out without the lines going ragged.

Both threads are done. Summary:

**The ink pass is in and verified.** Knockout now reduces every plate to luminance and applies a fixed ink curve (levels 40/235, gamma 0.9) after the ground division — chosen from a three-way prototype and damage-checked at 1:1 against the finest hatching (hires sky) and stipple (base-res interior wall): nothing drops out, ground haze clears to true white, near-blacks settle to ink. In situ the interior plate now reads as black ink printed with the text — the wash-mid softness you flagged is gone. Side benefit: the PDF fell from 42MB to 12MB on single-channel plates. Also fixed en route: the pre-commit hook's trigger set didn't include knockout.py, so rendering-policy edits weren't rebuilding the book — it does now.

**The production memo on full-page plates is back** (preserved at `scratch/plate-leaves-memo-2026-07-18.md`) and it's a genuinely good piece of consulting. The short version:

- **What we built is the wood-engraved trade-book convention, correctly** — cuts locked into the forme, printed with the text, versos live, no captions. Dedicated plate leaves with blank versos are historically the *steel-engraving* convention; full conversion would import the wrong bibliography.
- **But it found our own format doctrine half-implemented**: the ruling already declares journal-side portraits "full-page plates," yet they render as 85% inline cuts that get a page to themselves only by breaking luck — morrow-hollow currently shares its page with "This is the end of my account," and fifty-yards shares the book's final image with text.
- **Recommendation: the doctrinal hybrid** — promote exactly the five portraits (first-sighting, offering-stake, morrow-hollow, journal-found, fifty-yards) to full leaves, versos live, folios counted-but-unprinted per the gatefold's house rule, no captions, no recto-forcing; the thirteen landscapes and the gatefold stay inline. It notes this makes the portrait grammar legible: portrait leaf = the journal's voice, landscape cut = Farrell's forensic eye, with the two late Farrell portraits enacting the inheritance. Cost: +3–5 pages.
- **Its one hard gate — portrait resolution (208 ppi at full measure) — is exactly what the hires protocol now dissolves**: the 2× pass takes portraits to ~415 ppi at full measure. The memo also specs the three assemble.py changes (a `\fullplate` command on the gatefold's skeleton, a pinning-doctrine amendment, and a build-enforced ppi assertion).

Natural sequencing if you want the hybrid: run the full-set hires pass first (it's required regardless), then the leaf promotion is pure layout. Your call on hybrid (a) — and on whether it happens before or after the review round starts.

The ladder's verdict is honest but unwelcome: **strength can't reach the calf without breaking the plate.** d0.35 improves her from poodle-blob to lamb-ish and fixes the herd beautifully; d0.45 rounds her back; d0.55 starts bold-outlining the bulls toward comic illustration; and d0.65 is a full macro reroll — the entire cloud tower replaced by streaming cirrus, herd re-spaced, and the calf *still* woolly. She's a ~1cm figure at print scale sitting squarely in the model's white-woolly-quadruped attractor, and the refiner redraws everything around her before it redraws her.

**My recommendation: adopt d0.35** — consistent with the other four leaves, herd morphology genuinely fixed, hold intact — and log the calf as the accepted soft it has already been through ten instrument rounds, with one note in its favor: "an autumn calf, born when no calf is born" carries a little wrongness honestly. The one genuine escalation left isn't strength, it's *regional*: a ControlNet-inpaint pass masked to the calf under the same scene prompt (the calf tokens are already in it — no prompt tweaks). That's new tooling with an extra model download and uncertain payoff; I'd bank it as a possible experiment rather than a gate.

Adopt d0.35 and build both artifacts, or hold for the inpaint experiment first?

## ASSISTANT

The catalog confirms the plan was pre-seeded: the tracks image was re-cut *as* the cover device — "the boards carry the book's true device — the pursuit as inscription... Composition leaves the upper field open for the deferred cover typography." Neither walker appears; it's the promise, not the payoff. So the rough plan is executing a standing design, not improvising one. The design space as I see it, with the title page unpinned alongside:

**The subtitle question first, because it has a doctrine collision in it.** The "more verbose claim of what the book is purported to be" — the period long-subtitle ("Being an account of…, together with passages from the journal of…") — would put a provenance claim on the outermost surface of the book. That doesn't just cost verbosity; it *enacts the compiler frame*, which we ruled never-enact three days ago precisely because the compiler question is twice-certified as productively unsettled. The book's paratext already has a clean two-layer grammar: period text inside, honest modern apparatus outside (the Lakota statement, the AI notice, the repo pointer). The cover is the outermost layer — it belongs to the honest-modern side. So the choices that respect the standing rulings are "A novella" (honest label, already the title page's word) or **no genre marker at all** — my lean, since the quietest cover claims nothing and lets the title page carry the label where it already lives.

**Four directions:**

1. **The plan — full-bleed tracks image, type in the open sky.** Title + authors in the upper field the image reserved. Strongest thumbnail and shelf presence; the whole book in one emblem before it's opened. The image doing double duty as frontispiece has no period problem (and dropping the interior frontispiece would cost the two-trails overture facing the title, which I'd keep). *My recommendation.*

2. **Cloth-binding pastiche** — the most period-honest as *object*: solid stamped-cloth ground, gilt-style title, small blind-stamped vignette (the stake, or the tracks reduced to a device). An 1880s trade binding, which is exactly what the Aldridge-edition fanon would have produced. Risks: faux gilt reads costume when it misses, and it surrenders the image entirely at thumbnail size.

3. **All-type wrapper** — nineteenth-century paper-wrapper/title-page cover, rules and letterpress only. Quiet and cheap to execute well; but it's also where the verbose period claim would naturally live, and per the above I'd keep that door shut.

4. **Framed-plate variant** — the tracks image as a bordered plate on a quiet ground, type above the frame rather than over the sky. This is the book's own internal grammar (boundary is whitespace, plates are framed cuts) extended to the boards; it also sidesteps any type-over-image legibility risk. The compromise candidate if full-bleed type placement fights the image.

**Title page pairing:** unpinned, it should simply follow the cover's register — if the cover is letterspaced Pagella over the sky (option 1/4), the current variant-A title page already matches and needs nothing; if you went cloth-pastiche, the title page could take more period furniture, with the same enactment caution applying to any long-title text.

**Production notes regardless of direction:** cover-tracks needs its up-resolution first, and it's squarely in the drift-prone class (snow field + sky = tonal everything), so plan on the two-round recipe. And the type should *never* be baked into the raster — image below, typography as vector overlay at assembly time, so title tweaks don't reroll the image and the lettering stays crisp at any size. The eventual deliverable set is three-fold: EPUB cover raster, canonical front board, and the POD full wrap (front/spine/back with barcode zone) as its own artifact.

Pick a direction and I'll start with the cover-tracks up-resolution, then mock the typography as an overlay for your eye.

## ASSISTANT

All three fixed, adopted, and committed (a43e780):

- **speaking-to-her** — root cause found and fixed structurally: the refiner never loaded scene LoRAs, so it was refining a LoRA-born Morrow with the base model's prior — hence the hipster. `hires_refine` now honors catalog `lora` fields; adopted at d0.15+LoRA, where the striped blanket-coat and wild beard survive (d0.25 was already converting him to a jacket).
- **morrow-witnessed** — adopted at d0.25 with the LoRA pull restoring the walker's gaunt profile and the herd stepping back from photorealism; the horizon watcher, which the refiner hallucinated in *every* refined cell, is excised with a feathered same-row horizon clone. That's the campaign's only manual pixel intervention, and it's recorded as such in the catalog rather than passed off as generation.
- **frozen-man** — the skipped middle cell (single-round d0.25) was the right one all along: base sky hatching and snow texture kept, none of the two-round's over-fine stipple, hand intact.

Both books rebuilt clean, folios stable. The plates stand production-final again — now with the LoRA lesson and the ghost precedent banked in the doctrine for anything the wrap session's fresh eyes may flag.

Both settled and committed (537f5d2):

- **frozen-man** lands at d0.15 — the full strength ladder is now on the record for this plate (0.35 washed the snow, two-round over-refined it, 0.25 close, 0.15 right), which is useful calibration data: the most tonal plates want the least intervention.
- **morrow-witnessed reverts to the blessed base** — the only plate of nineteen to refuse refinement entirely. The evidence was complete: the walker loses his hair at low strengths and his gauntness at middle ones, a watcher hallucinates onto the horizon at d0.25+, and the bulls were born tonal, so no strength can engrave them — only smooth them. At 304 ppi inline the base passes every gate the build enforces. The fallback clause existed for exactly this case, and the catalog records the full ladder so nobody re-litigates it with fresh optimism later.

Eighteen plates hires, one deliberately base, both books rebuilt clean. If the herd's photo-realism in the *base* still bothers you at print scale, the only remaining road is a fresh generation sweep for that scene — but that reopens a blessed plate, so it's yours to call, and "the plate that refused" is a perfectly respectable entry in the working record as it stands.
